keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: [gu] is pronounced as in 'preguntar' and [j] is pronounced as in 'ojo'.
Words ending in a vowel, -n or -s have penultimate syllable stress unless they have an accent.
Words ending in a consonant other than -n or -s have final syllable stress unless they have an accent.
Plural reflexive verbs can express a reciprocal action when people are doing the action to each other.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Spanish words ending in a consonant other than -n or -s show final syllable stress unless otherwise indicated by an accent.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Spanish words ending in a consonant other than -n or -s always show final syllable stress.

lessonKeywords.description: describes an action where the subject and object of the verb are the same
used to indicate doing something to yourself, words like 'myself' and 'yourself'
shows who something belongs to
replaces a possessive adjective and a noun

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Reflexive verbs have the same subject and object.
To conjugate plural reflexive verbs, place the pronouns 'nos', 'os' and 'se' before verbs with the corresponding ending.
Possessive adjectives show who something belongs to and possessive pronouns replace possessive adjectives + nouns.
The possessive adjectives 'mío', 'tuyo' and 'suyo' can follow 'ser' to show belonging to, e.g. 'la bolsa es mía'.
To form possessive pronouns, use the definite article before 'mío', 'suyo' or 'tuyo', based on gender and number.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Verbs do not always have different subjects and objects. For example, reflexive verbs have the same subject and object.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Verbs must always have different subjects and objects.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use plural reflexive verbs, possessive adjectives and pronouns in the context of daily life.

lessonKeywords.description: shows who something belongs to
replaces a possessive adjective and a noun

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Possessive adjectives show who something belongs to.
'Mío', 'tuyo', 'suyo', 'nuestro' and 'vuestro' are possessive adjectives in Spanish and can be used after 'ser'.
Possessive pronouns replace a possessive adjective and a noun.
'El mío', 'el tuyo', 'el suyo', 'el nuestro' and 'el vuestro' are possessive pronouns in Spanish.
Possessive adjectives and pronouns change to reflect the grammatical gender and number of the thing possessed.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The Spanish translation of 'the money is hers' is 'el dinero es suyo' because the object is masculine. Possessive adjectives agree with the object, not the owner.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The Spanish translation of 'the money is hers' (for exampl) is 'el dinero es suya' because the owner is feminine.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use possessive adjectives and pronouns within the context of holidays and travel.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Learning Cycles 2 and 3 include Higher-tier grammatical concepts.

lessonKeywords.description: verb tense used to describe habitual actions in the present, e.g. 'I speak'
verb tense used to express completed actions in the past, e.g. 'I spoke'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: To conjugate plural forms of -ar verbs in the simple present, remove the -ar and add -amos, -áis, -an.
To conjugate plural forms of -ar verbs in the preterite, remove the -ar and add -amos, -asteis, -aron.
Verb endings and time markers can help us to distinguish between past and present time frames in Spanish.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The ending -amos also corresponds to the 1st person plural form of the preterite for -ar verbs. Therefore, 'hablamos' can also mean 'we spoke'. The context of the verb should clarify which is the correct translation.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The only translation of 'hablamos' is 'we speak'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can distinguish between past and present in the context of life at home.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: It is important to respond to role-play prompts with a short phrase or sentence.
Interrogatives can be used to ask questions in a role-play scenario.
Useful interrogatives in Spanish are: '¿cuándo?', '¿cómo?', '¿dónde?', '¿cuánto?', '¿qué?' and '¿hay?'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: It is not necessary to give long, developed answers to role-play prompts. It is best to respond using a short phrase or sentence.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Verbs ending in -er and -ir have the same endings in the preterite tense.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: To conjugate reflexive verbs, place the pronouns 'me', 'te', 'se', 'nos', 'os' or 'se' before the conjugated verb.
Indirect object pronouns precede conjugated verbs in 1-verb structures, e.g. 'me hablan todos los días'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: 'Por' can mean several things in Spanish. For example, in addition to 'for', it can also mean 'by' and 'in' in certain contexts.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: There are two ways to say 'I am' in Spanish. These are 'estoy' (for location, mood and temporary state) and 'soy' (for general traits).

possessive adjective 'his, 'her' or 'its' for plural nouns

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Spanish words ending in a vowel, -n, or -s naturally have penultimate syllable stress, e.g. 'vamos' and 'mundo'.
If a word ending in a different consonant has penultimate syllable stress, there is an accent on the stressed vowel.
Some Spanish verbs have a completely different meaning when used with a reflexive pronoun, e.g. 'quedar' and 'quedarse'.
The reflexive pronoun 'se' means 'himself', 'herself' or 'itself' before a verb, e.g. 'se lava' ('he washes himself').
To say 'his', 'her', 'its' before a noun we use the possessive adjectives 'su' (m, f singular) or 'sus' (m, f plural).

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In Spanish there are many reflexive verbs and they are not just used to describe routine activities. This lesson includes the verb 'acordar' ('to agree') compared with the reflexive verb 'acordarse' ('to remember').
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Reflexive verbs are just for routine activities.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the reflexive pronoun 'se' before a range of verbs in the context of describing the Mexican custom 'Day of the Dead'.

teacherTips.teacherTip: To adapt the C4 speaking task for pupils who need more support, teachers could provide the full Spanish sentences, so that pupil B chooses the correct ending after hearing 'su(s)' or 'se' and pupil A writes the English meaning.

lessons.lessonTitle: People and places in Mexico: possessive adjective 'su'
lessons.unitTitle: Everyday life: possessive adjectives, pronouns

lessonKeywords.description: word that goes before a noun to show ownership or belonging
possessive adjective 'his', 'her', 'its' (singular)
possessive adjective 'his', 'her', 'its' (plural)

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Mexico is famous for many things including its artists, its archaeology, its food, its customs and its unique history.
Possessive adjectives go before nouns to show belonging and ownership.
'Su' is 'his', 'hers' or 'its' before a singular noun, e.g. 'su país' - 'his, her, its country'.
'Sus' is 'his', 'hers', or 'its' before a plural noun, e.g. 'sus padres' - 'his, her, its parents'.
As 'su' and 'sus' have different meanings, you will often need context to translate them accurately.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: 'Su' is his', 'hers' or 'its' before a singular noun. 'Sus' is 'his' 'hers', or 'its' before a plural noun.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: 'Su' is the only possessive adjective for 'his' and 'hers' in Spanish.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can understand the different uses of the possessive adjective 'su' in the context of learning about people and places in Mexico.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Mexico is a fascinating country that can be explored to show further extraordinary examples of wonderful Latin culture and customs.

lessons.lessonTitle: People and places: 'ser' and 'estar' singular and plural persons
lessons.unitTitle: People and places: 'ser' and 'estar'

lessonKeywords.description: vowel that is not strong or dominant in pronunciation. e.g. the letter [u]
vowel that is strong in pronunciation. e.g. [a], [e], [o]
verb 'to be, being' used to describe permanent traits
verb 'to be, being' used to describe temporary state/mood and location

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The weak vowel [i] when next to  [a], [e] and [o] become a single syllable.
The verb 'ser' means 'to, be, being' and it is used to describe permanent traits.
The verb 'estar' means 'to, be, being' and it is used to describe temporary states/moods.
In Spanish, adjectives must agree with the nouns they accompany in gender and number.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: When a weak vowel is next to a strong vowel, like for example [i] next to [a], [e] or [o], it merges with them to make a single syllable.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: When a weak vowel is next to a strong vowel, we pronounce them separately.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe places and people using a variety of adjectives and the verbs ‘ser’ and ‘estar’.

teacherTips.teacherTip: For Task A2, the teacher might want to play just one round and put all the sentences on one slide.

lessons.lessonTitle: People: 'ser' and 'estar' singular persons
lessons.unitTitle: People and places: 'ser' and 'estar'

lessonKeywords.description: vowel that is not strong or dominant in pronunciation, e.g. the letter [u]
verb 'to be, being' used to describe permanent traits
verb 'to be, being' used to describe temporary state/mood and location

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The weak vowel [u] when next to [a], [e] and [o] becomes a single syllable.
The verb 'ser' means 'to, be, being' and it is used to describe permanent traits.
The verb 'estar' means 'to, be, being' and it is used to describe temporary states/moods.
Adjectives like 'listo' and 'malo' have different meanings depending on which verb is used: 'ser' or 'estar'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The verb 'ser' is used to talk about permanent traits, and the verb 'estar' is used to talk about temporary states/moods and location.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: It doesn't matter which Spanish translation of the verb 'to be' we use, as they both mean 'to be, being'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can talk about people's traits and states using 'ser' and 'estar'.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The teacher might want to set a different time limit for task B1.

lessons.lessonTitle: What is it? Singular indefinite articles 'un' and 'una'
lessons.unitTitle: Belongings: 'tener' and articles 'un' and 'una'

lessonKeywords.description: pronounced as in ‘libro’ and ‘llamar’
a word for an thing or person (car, eye)
the  'a' that comes before a noun (a tree, a car)
all nouns in Spanish are masculine or feminine, even if they are not about people/animals

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: [l] sounds the same in English and Spanish, but [ll] sounds different in Spanish.
Nouns and indefinite articles have grammatical gender in Spanish.
Most masculine nouns end in 'o' and most feminine nouns end in 'a'.
'Un' means a/an with masculine nouns, and 'una' is a/an with feminine nouns.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: [ll] is pronounced differently in Spanish and English. It is important to recognise and pronounce sound-spelling links correctly to understand and be understood by other Spanish speakers.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: [ll] is pronounced the same in Spanish and English.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can recognise the gender of nouns and use the singular indefinite articles, 'un' and 'una', in Spanish.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The concept of gender is central to this lesson as we introduce grammatical gender of nouns and indefinite articles.  This can be linked to prior learning about gender-based spelling changes to adjectives.

lessons.lessonTitle: Conversations: 'estar', 'ser', 'tener' singular persons
lessons.unitTitle: Belongings: 'tener' and articles 'un' and 'una'

lessonKeywords.description: to have, having
Spanish question word 'what'
'some' for plural feminine nouns
'some' for plural masculine nouns

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Raise your voice at the end of a statement to ask a yes/no question with 'tener'. ‘¿Tienes …?’ is ‘Do you have?'.
'Qué' means 'what'; to ask ‘What do you have?’ use ‘¿Qué tienes?’.
'Unas' is 'some' for plural feminine nouns; 'unos' is ‘some’ for plural masculine nouns.
Conversations involve careful listening and knowing vocabulary securely, especially key verbs 'estar', 'ser', 'tener'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Spanish questions are easy to form. Yes/no questions have the same words as statements; to make a question you raise the pitch of your voice.  Information questions just add a question word, e.g. 'Qué ... ?' in front of the verb.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Spanish needs a word for 'do' in questions, e.g. 'Do you have?' and 'What do you have?'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can ask and answer questions using singular 'estar', 'ser' and 'tener' about things that I or someone else has.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The simplicity of Spanish questions can become clearer for pupils if they imagine a Spanish person trying to learn to ask English questions and having to add in 'do' or 'does', when there is no meaning 'do' attached to it. How would 'Do you do sport?' translate for a Spanish learner of English?

lessons.lessonTitle: What people have: plural indefinite articles 'unos' and 'unas'
lessons.unitTitle: Belongings: 'tener' and articles 'un' and 'una'

lessonKeywords.description: pronounced as in 'casa'
pronounced as in 'comer'
pronounced as in 'escuchar'
'some' for feminine plural nouns
'some' for masculineplural nouns

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The sounds [ca], [co], [cu] are pronounced as in casa, coche, escuchar.
Add 's' to make a Spanish word plural, if it ends in a vowel.
To say 'some' for plural masculine nouns use 'unos'. For plural feminine nouns use 'unas'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: There are two words for 'some' in Spanish, just as there are two words for 'a/an'. 'Unos' is 'some' for plural masculine nouns.  'Unas' is 'some' for plural feminine nouns.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: There is just one word for 'some' in Spanish.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can form plural nouns and use 'unos' and 'unas' to talk about more than one.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Teachers may consider entering pupils in Y7 for the Foreign Language Spelling Bee competition. It has four stages: class, whole school, regional and national. The words that pupils have to learn are all high frequency and also on the GCSE word list, so the competition is a great start to learning.

lessons.lessonTitle: What people have: 'tener' singular persons, alphabet
lessons.unitTitle: Belongings: 'tener' and articles 'un' and 'una'

lessonKeywords.description: 'eñe', a unique letter of the Spanish alphabet
Spanish verb 'to have, having'
verb forms for ‘I’, ‘you’ and ‘she, he, it’

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The Spanish alphabet has 27 letters, including the letter ñ which is not in the English alphabet.
The Spanish alphabet letter names have patterns: letter + e, e + letter + e. There are eight irregular letter names.
The singular verb forms of 'tener' are: 'tengo' - I have, 'tienes' - you have, 'tiene' - she, he, it has.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The verbs 'tengo', 'tienes' and 'tiene' mean 'I have', 'you have' and 'she, he, it has'. You do not need to use separate pronouns 'I', 'you', 'she, he, it'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: To say 'I have', 'you have', 'she, he, it has' you need the words for 'I', 'you' and 'she, he, it'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can understand what I, you and someone else has in Spanish.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Pupils will benefit from brief, but frequent revisiting of the Spanish alphabet.  One way to do this is to reprieve the song.  Playing a previously learnt song at the beginning of the lesson is a great way to help pupils settle quickly and tune in to the sounds of the new language.

lessons.lessonTitle: Quedar con los amigos: 'hacer' singular present, indirect object pronouns
lessons.unitTitle: Lifestyle and wellbeing: la vida de todos los días

lessonKeywords.description: pronounced as in 'calle'
an irregular verb meaning to do, make, doing or making
word for a person, place, or thing
word that gives information about a noun
form of the verb giving its general meaning, with no subject or tense

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: [l] and [ll] do not sound the same in Spanish. [ll] is pronounced as in ‘calle’.
Classifying words by parts of speech is one useful strategy for consolidating vocabulary.
Hacer is an irregular verb. The singular forms are ‘hago’, I do/make, ‘haces’, you do/make, ‘hace’, she, he does/makes.
We use ‘hace’ to talk about the weather: hace calor/frío/etc. This translates as ‘it is’ in English.
Check verbs, nouns and adjectives, word order, little words and idiomacy when translating into Spanish.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: It's important to remember that Spanish uses the verb 'hacer' when talking about the weather. For example, 'it's cold' translates as 'hace frío'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: When talking about the weather, I can translate directly from English (e.g. 'it's cold').

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the verb 'hacer' in a range of contexts to talk about school.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Teachers might decide to guide pupils through the translation task, completing each sentence at a time or challenge students by giving them the checklist and encourage them to use it to tackle the translation independently.

lessons.lessonTitle: ¿Qué te pasa? Indirect object pronouns and 'doler'
lessons.unitTitle: Lifestyle and wellbeing: la vida de todos los días

lessonKeywords.description: replaces the person(s) or thing(s) receiving the action of the verb, when the meaning is 'to' or 'for' someone.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The definite article is used with body parts rather than ‘my’ ‘yours’, ‘his’/’her’, etc.
‘Doler’ (to hurt, to be painful) is very commonly used with an indirect object pronoun.
In sentences with ‘doler’, the subject is the body part(s) so you need to use the correct verb ending for -er verbs.
In a role play, you are expected to say a few words or a short phrase in response to each prompt/bullet.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: It's important to say a few words or a short phrase/sentence in response to each prompt/bullet rather than one-word answers.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: One-word answers are sufficient in the role play.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use indirect object pronouns and body parts to talk about what hurts.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Teachers can use a timer to ensure students get used to preparing this under time-limited circumstances. It's important for students to understand that they don't need to memorise their answers as they will be reading from their preparation notes.

lessons.lessonTitle: En una fiesta de cumpleaños: modals, direct object pronouns in 2-verb structures
lessons.unitTitle: Lifestyle and wellbeing: la vida de todos los días

lessonKeywords.description: a verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in the infinitive, e.g., 'must do', 'can eat', 'want to help'
form of the verb giving its general meaning, with no subject or tense
replaces a noun that is the object of the sentence

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The modal verbs 'querer', 'poder', 'deber' and 'tener que' are followed by an infinitive verb.
In 2-verb structures, direct object pronouns can go before the conjugated verb and attached to the infinitive.
When using verbs in the negative form with direct object pronouns, the 'no' needs to go before the object pronoun.
[z] sounds like 'zapato' and [co] sounds like 'coche'. Pay attention to these two key sounds in words like 'conozco'.
The translation for 'saber’ + infinitive is ‘can’, meaning ‘to know how to’ do something.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Modal verbs are followed by the infinitive.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Modal verbs are followed by a conjugated verb which changes its ending to match the person who is speaking.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use use the modal verbs ‘querer’, ‘poder’, ‘deber’ and ‘tener que' to talk about a birthday party.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Students should be giving sufficient time to prepare for the speaking task before completing it. Engaging pupils in the thinking process of planning both the language and the ideas is key to develop their fluency. Students can read what they have prepared or attempt to say it from memory.

lessons.lessonTitle: En una fiesta de cumpleaños: adjective position and agreement
lessons.unitTitle: Lifestyle and wellbeing: la vida de todos los días

lessonKeywords.description: a way to categorise all nouns as feminine or masculine
adjectives that can go before the noun

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Adjectives need to agree in gender and number with the noun that they describe.
'Mismo', 'último', 'propio', 'primero', 'segundo' and 'tercer' are examples of prenominal adjectives.
Some prenominal adjectives lose the –o ending before a singular masculine noun: primer, tercer, buen, mal.
The position of adjectives changes its meaning. This happens with 'grande', 'único', 'pobre' and 'viejo'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: There are some adjectives that can also go before the noun and these are called prenominal adjectives.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All adjectives go after the noun in Spanish.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use adjectives correctly when describing a birthday party

teacherTips.teacherTip: Teachers can provide students with the list of vocabulary included in additional materials and encourage them to use up as many of those as possible as part of the speaking task. This would provide students the opportunity to practise vocabulary from the GCSE word list in writing and speaking.

lessons.lessonTitle: Planes para una fiesta: singular present -er/-ir, direct object pronouns
lessons.unitTitle: Lifestyle and wellbeing: la vida de todos los días

lessonKeywords.description: describes habitual events in the present: 'I do'
does not follow the regular rules
replace a noun that is the object of the sentence
are used to identify a specific noun or to refer to a noun that has already been specified

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Present tense -er/-ir verbs in 1st, 2nd, 3rd person singular (-o, -es, -e).
Verbs that end in –cer or –cir that have a spelling change in the 1st person singular. We add a 'z' before the 'co'.
Direct object pronouns (lo, la, los, las) come before the verb.
Use 'lo' to mean 'him' or 'it' (for masculine objects) and 'la' to mean 'her' or 'it' (for feminine objects).
Use 'los' to mean 'them' (for masculine objects) and 'las' to mean 'them' (for feminine objects).

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remember that direct object pronouns (lo, la, los and las) come before a verb. 'El' is the masculine singular form of the definite article 'the'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: 'El' and 'lo' are interchangeable, as 'la' (article) and 'la' (DOP) and 'las' (article) and 'las' (DOP) look exactly the same.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the present tense of -er and -ir verbs and direct object pronouns to talk about what people do at a party.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Students should be giving sufficient time to prepare for the speaking task before completing it.

lessons.lessonTitle: En el colegio: indirect object pronouns in 2-verb structures
lessons.unitTitle: Lifestyle and wellbeing: la vida de todos los días

lessonKeywords.description: letters [a], [e] and [o]
letters [i] and [u]
replaces the person(s) or thing(s) receiving the action of the verb, when the meaning is 'to' or 'for' someone

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: When weak vowels [i] and [u] appear next to a strong vowel, [a], [e] and [o], they make a single syllable.
‘Doler’ (to hurt, to be painful) is very commonly used with an indirect object pronoun.
Me (to me), te (to you, singular) and le (to him, her, it) are the singular indirect object pronouns.
Nos (to us), os (to you, plural) and les (to them) are the plural indirect object pronouns.
Indirect object pronouns can go before the conjugated verb or attached to the infinitive in two-verb constructions.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Spanish word order is different to English. Indirect object pronouns come before the conjugated verb. With 2-verb structures, they can go before the first verb or after the infinitive, attached to it.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Spanish word order is identical to English so I can translate sentences with indirect object pronouns literally from one language to another.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use indirect object pronouns and 2-verb structures to talk about a school day.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Giving a notional time for both speaking and writing tasks is a useful way to encourage pupils to speed up mental processing and increase spoken fluency. Teachers can also make use of mini whiteboards in order to check students' understanding, addressing gaps in their knowledge appropriately.

lessons.lessonTitle: Los días de colegio: present -er verbs, indirect object pronouns
lessons.unitTitle: Lifestyle and wellbeing: la vida de todos los días

lessonKeywords.description: have a spelling change in the stem
replaces the person(s) or thing(s) receiving the action of the verb, when the meaning is 'to' or 'for' someone

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Stem-changing verbs like 'pedir', 'querer' and 'poder' have a spelling change in singular persons and 3rd person plural.
Present '-ER' verbs in 1st, 2nd and 3rd person plural have the ending -emos, -éis, -en.
Indirect object pronouns replace the receiver of the action of the verb, when the meaning is 'to me', 'for you'.
Use 'me' if the person affected by the verb is 'me', 'te' if it's you and 'le' if it's him, her or it.
Spanish sentences can start with the subject or with the object.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Spanish sentences can start with the subject or with the indirect object. This is important when using indirect object pronouns as they can come before the verb (e.g. 'me interesan las matemáticas').
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Spanish sentences always start with the subject.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the present tense and indirect object pronouns when talking about a school day.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Teachers might make use of mini whiteboards for writing tasks in order to guide student practice and check  students' understanding, addressing gaps in their knowledge appropriately.

lessons.lessonTitle: Internet: 'interesar'-type verbs, pronouns after prepositions
lessons.unitTitle: Media and technology: Internet y yo

lessonKeywords.description: group of verbs which require the use of an indirect object pronoun
refers to a person or thing that is indirectly affected by the verb, e.g. 'to me', 'to her', 'to them', etc.
a word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word
used to emphasise a person or after certain prepositions

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: 'Interesar'-type verbs express likes, emotions, interests - they work differently to normal Spanish verbs.
Instead of saying 'I am interested in something', we say 'something interests me' - 'me interesan estas aplicaciones.'
'Interesar'-type verbs agree with the subject, the ‘interesting thing(s)’; indirect object ‘me’ shows who is interested.
Emphatic pronouns are used after prepositions such as 'a', 'para' 'sin', 'sobre', 'con'.
When used after 'a' before an 'interesar'-type verb, emphatic pronouns emphasise the person affected by the verb.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Indirect object pronouns refer to a person or thing indirectly affected by the verb and go before 'interesar'-type verbs, while emphatic pronouns are used for emphasis after prepositions.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Indirect object pronouns are the same as emphatic pronouns.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use 'interesar'-type verbs and pronouns after prepositions to talk about the internet.

teacherTips.teacherTip: English considers the word 'internet' to be a common noun now so we do not capitalise it. It is capitalised in Spanish and is often used without an article.

lessons.lessonTitle: ¿A quién sigues en redes? Photo card
lessons.unitTitle: Communication and the world around us: Internet y yo

lessonKeywords.description: acronym for photo description tasks (people and objects, action, location, mood)
an explanation or reason given for something that has been stated
a comparison made to show the differences between two or more things, people, or ideas

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: When describing photos in Spanish, it is important to convey a range of information.
The PALM acronym is a useful prompt to include a range of information when describing photos.
When describing photos in Spanish, it is important to use full sentences with verbs.
To make a photo description more interesting and complex, add justifications and contrasts.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: When describing photos in Spanish, it is important to use full sentences with verbs. To make the description even more interesting and complex add justifications and contrasts.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: I can describe a photo using single words.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can talk about my and other people's habits related to social media.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The teacher might want to turn this into a real classroom competition. This will boost engagement, and will give students a clear reason to aim high.

lessons.lessonTitle: Una peli de Guillermo del Toro: imperfect and preterite tenses
lessons.unitTitle: Media and technology: Internet y yo

lessonKeywords.description: verb tense used to talk about something that used to happen repeatedly and to set the scene in past-tense accounts
verb tense used to talk about something completed in the past and to drive the narrative forward in past-tense accounts
form of pronouns and verbs used to refer to 'she', 'he', 'it' (singular) or ‘they’ (plural)

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The imperfect tense is used for descriptions, giving background information and ongoing events in the past.
The preterite tense is used for completed events in the past.
We use the 3rd person singular and plural when we talk about a film.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: We use the imperfect to set the scene, to give background information and to describe onling states. And we use the preterite to express completed actions that move the plot forward.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: To describe the past we can use both the preterite and the imperfect interchangeably.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the imperfect and preterite tenses to describe a film.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The teacher might want to show students the trailer of 'El Laberinto del Fauno'.

lessons.lessonTitle: Las redes sociales y yo: conversation practice

lessonKeywords.description: express a person's thoughts, feelings, judgments, or beliefs rather than objective facts, e.g. 'I like', 'I prefer', 'I believe that'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Question words are essential when asking and understanding questions about social media.
It is important to develop answers to questions by using a variety of opinions, justifications and contrasting ideas.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: [que] is pronounced as in the word 'porque', and [cue] as in the word 'cuerpo'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: [que] and [cue] are pronounced the same.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can write and talk about how I and others use social media.

teacherTips.teacherTip: If time allows, the teacher could consider rearranging the classroom to facilitate a speed dating-style activity.

lessons.lessonTitle: La inteligencia artificial: 'tener' meaning 'be'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The verb 'tener' means 'to have, having'. Its forms are: 'tengo', 'tienes', 'tiene', 'tenemos', 'tenéis', 'tienen'.
An idiom is a phrase which does not translate word-for-word into another language.
The idiomatic expression 'tener' + noun is translated as 'to be' + adjective in English.
The term 'artificial intelligence', 'la inteligencia artificial (IA)' in Spanish, was coined by scientists in 1956.
AI use is now transforming daily lives; we can use 'tener' + noun expressions to discuss benefits and concerns with AI.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The idiomatic expression 'tener' + noun is translated in English as 'to be' + adjective.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: 'Tener' + noun always translates in English as 'to have' + noun.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can talk about how I and others use artificial intelligence in our daily lives using idiomatic expressions with 'tener'.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The teacher might want to ask students to write the words in activity A1 instead of saying them.

lessons.lessonTitle: La última película que vi: extend writing
lessons.unitTitle: Media and technology: Internet y yo

lessonKeywords.description: verb tense used to describe the setting, characters or things that were happening in the background during the film
verb tense used to talk about specific actions or events that happened and ended during the film

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The imperfect is used to give background information and for repeated actions in the past.
The preterite tense is used to talk about completed actions in the past.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The imperfect is used to set the scene, give background information and for repeated actions in the past and the preterite to say what happened, talk about completed events and actions in the past.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: For completed events and actions in the past I can use either the preterite or the imperfect.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the imperfect and the preterite tenses to write about the last film I watched.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The teacher may consider showing students the trailer for Icíar Bollaín's film El Olivo.

To refer to one person or thing indirectly affected by an action, use 'le'.
If more than one person or thing is indirectly affected, use 'les'.
When reading words aloud in Spanish, stress the penultimate syllable for any word ending in a vowel, -n or -s.
If the word has a written accent, stress the syllable with the accent.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: 'Le' means 'to him', 'to her' or 'to it' regardless of the person receiving the action, e.g. 'le doy un regalo a Lucía' or 'le doy un regalo a Daniel'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The indirect object pronoun 'le' changes to 'la' to match the gender of the person receiving the action.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Indirect object pronouns ('to, for him', 'them') indicate the person or thing that is indirectly affected by the verb.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: We use direct object pronouns to avoid repeating nouns. In Spanish they usually go before the verb.
Masculine DOPs are ‘lo’, meaning ‘him' or 'it’, and ‘los’, meaning ‘them’.
Feminine DOPs are ‘la’, meaning ‘her' or 'it’, and ‘las’, meaning ‘them’.
The verbs ‘probar’, ‘costar’ and ‘soler’ are stem changing verbs. When conjugated, their stem changes from 'o' to 'ue'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In Spanish, the direct object pronoun usually goes before the verb, e.g. 'pruebas el chocolate caliente' - 'lo pruebas.'

lessons.lessonTitle: In class and at home: modal verb 'debemos'

lessonKeywords.description: pronouncing the second-last syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word
verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in the infinitive, e.g. 'must', 'can', 'want'
modal verb that means 'to have to', 'must'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Rules about penultimate (syllable) stress tell us if we need to write an accent on the penultimate vowel.
Applying knowledge about syllable stress helps to remember how to say words that we may have forgotten how to pronounce.
'Deber' is a modal verb meaning 'to have to, must'. It is conjugated as a regular -er verb; the 'we' form is 'debemos'.
The verb deber is always followed by an infinitive, e.g. 'Siempre debemos decir la verdad.'

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: English confuses us here. We say 'I must go' rather than 'I must to go' as English uses an infinitive but without 'to'. In Spanish, after modal verbs 'deber', 'poder' and 'querer' the 2nd verb must always be an infinitive; 'I must go' is 'Debo ir'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: When there are two verbs together, e.g. 'I must go', we need to conjugate both.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use modal verbs 'deber' and 'poder' to understand and write about what I and others must and can do in class and at home.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The extended listening activity can be easily differentiated by: i) reducing or increasing the number of questions overall or ii) by removing the ‘story doesn’t say’ column. The audio can be paused to provide additional support.

lessons.lessonTitle: Activities: plural 'hacer' and subject pronouns
lessons.unitTitle: Comparing what people do: -ER and -IR verbs

lessonKeywords.description: pronouncing the final syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word
Spanish verb meaning 'to do, doing' or to make, making'
represents the person, people or thing(s) doing the verb e.g. 'I', 'we', 'they'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Applying the two rules about final syllable stress enables correct use of accents when transcribing.
Listening to familiar language in new contexts and transcribing it deepens vocabulary knowledge.
'Hacer', irregular in its I form ‘hago’, is regular in other forms. We do, make is ‘hacemos’, they do, make is ‘hacen’.
Spanish subject pronouns add emphasis or clarity, e.g. nosotros hacemos los deberes, mientras que ellas hacen deporte.
‘We’ is nosotros for boys/men or mixed gender groups, nosotras for girls/women; ‘they’ also has two forms, ellos, ellas.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Spanish has two words each for ‘we’ and ‘they’. The plural pronoun ‘we’ is ‘nosotros’ for boys/men or mixed gender groups, ‘nosotras’ for girls/women; ‘they’ also has two forms, 'ellos' and 'ellas'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: There is just one word for ‘we’ and one word for ‘they’ in Spanish.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use subject pronouns and plural forms of ‘hacer’ to contrast activities that ‘we’ or ‘they’ do.

teacherTips.teacherTip: There are many ways to make listening less daunting, including: making it a pair activity (listen out for odd and even item numbers, then pair-share answers); encouraging silent rehearsal of the word or sentence heard to keep it longer in mind and allow time to process and understand the message.

lessons.lessonTitle: A party: -ir verbs in 1st person plural

lessonKeywords.description: pronouncing one syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word
verb whose infinitive form ends in -ir
form of pronouns and verbs used to refer to 'we'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Applying knowledge about syllable stress reminds us how to say words that we may have forgotten how to pronounce.
Reading aloud accurately supports our own and others’ vocabulary learning.
We can say we know a verb when we can compose sentences of our own with its different persons.
The verb endings for Spanish -er and -ir verbs are the same for 'I', 'you (singular)', 'she', 'he', 'it' and 'they'.
The 1st person plural ‘we’ ending for -ir verbs is -imos; for -er verbs it is -emos.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The verbs endings for Spanish -er and -ir verbs are the same for 'I', 'you (singular)', 'she', 'he', 'it' and 'they'. The 1st person plural ‘we’ ending for -er verbs is -emos, and for -ir verbs is -imos.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Spanish -er and -ir verbs share the same endings in the present tense.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use 1st person plural -ir verbs to talk about how we organise a party.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The speaking task in learning cycle 3 is a sentence-building activity; the focus is on pupils manipulating the new -ir verb forms from this lesson, and therefore the sentence endings are provided as phrases, to focus all of the cognitive load on the new forms.

lessons.lessonTitle: A party: simple present for immediate plans
lessons.unitTitle: Comparing what people do: -ER and -IR verbs

lessonKeywords.description: pronouncing one syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word
verb changed to match its subject and tense
verb changed to match its subject and tense

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Applying knowledge about syllable stress reminds us how to pronounce words we have not used for some time.
Recalling vocabulary with a partner is very effective, especially if we can support each other with accurate stress.
Conjugated verbs in the present tense have different stress from their infinitives.
Spanish uses the simple present for habitual actions, e.g. 'Siempre hago' - 'I always do'.
Spanish also uses the simple present for today’s immediate plans, e.g. 'Hoy hago' - 'Today I am doing'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The simple present in Spanish is used for habitual actions and immediate plans. '¿Qué haces hoy?' translates as 'What are you doing today?' - 'Hoy hago mis deberes.' 'Today I'm doing my homework'. English uses the present continuous here instead.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The simple present tense in Spanish is only for habitual actions, e.g. 'every week I do my homework'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use present tense verbs to write about preparations for a party.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The English message in the lesson scaffolds the pupils' ideas, whilst the focus on verbs supports language production. Teachers may want to provide additional support e.g. a copy of the additional materials, or challenge, by prompting them to use their personal repertoire or reference materials.

lessons.lessonTitle: In class and at home: modal verb 'podemos'
lessons.unitTitle: Comparing what people do: -ER and -IR verbs

lessonKeywords.description: pronouncing the second-last syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word
word that has the opposite meaning of another word
verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in the infinitive, e.g. must, can, want
modal verb that means to be able to/can

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Listening to words with final and penultimate syllable stress helps to develop the ability to identify the stress.
Making vocabulary links using antonyms or words with related meanings can enhance recall.
The verb 'poder' is a modal verb and means 'to be able to', 'can'.
Most present tense forms of 'poder' have a vowel change in the stem, ('puedo'); 'podemos' (we can) has no vowel change.
The verb 'poder' is always followed by an infinitive, e.g. 'Podemos participar en clase.'

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The 1st, 2nd, 3rd persons singular ('puedo', 'puedes', 'puede') and 3rd person plural ('pueden') forms all have a stem change from 'o' to 'ue' but 1st person plural 'we' form is 'podemos'; it keeps the same vowel as the infinitive 'poder'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All present tense forms of the model verb 'poder' have the same vowel change in the stem, o-> ue.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use an expanding range of words to talk about everyday activities that I and others can do in class and at home.

teacherTips.teacherTip: During the vocabulary focus in the 2nd learning cycle, teachers may want to remind pupils about their own 'vocabulario', or personal word repertoire, and encourage them to add any words that are important to them to the place set aside for this.

lessons.lessonTitle: Activities: singular 'hacer' and subject pronouns
lessons.unitTitle: Comparing what people do: -ER and -IR verbs

lessonKeywords.description: pronouncing the final syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word
Spanish verb meaning 'to do, doing' or 'to make, making'
irregular 1st person singular 'I' form of 'hacer' meaning 'I do, I make'
common pairing of verb and noun, e.g. 'make an effort'
represents the person, people or thing(s) doing the verb, e.g. 'I', 'we', 'they'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: If the stress is on the final syllable of a word ending in 'n' or 's' or a vowel, there is an accent on the last vowel.
Words ending in other consonants have final syllable stress and no accent, e.g. 'genial'.
'Hacer' means 'to do, make'. It is irregular in its 'I' form only; 'I do, I make' is 'hago'.
'Hacer' combines with many nouns to make common verb-noun phrases, e.g. 'Hago un esfuerzo'.
Subject pronouns add emphasis or clarity in Spanish; they are often used to contrast the actions of different people.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: English always uses subject pronouns. Spanish often relies on verb endings alone to indicate the 'doer'. However, Spanish has subject pronouns, e.g. 'yo' (I), 'tú' (you), 'él' (he), 'ella' (she), which are used for emphasis and clarity, as needed.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Subject pronouns, e.g. 'I', 'she', 'we', 'they', are used in the same way in Spanish and English.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use subject pronouns and singular forms of 'hacer' to contrast the activities I do with those you, she, or he does.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Creating verb-noun combinations from memory is an effective way to revisit sizeable numbers of words in one go. Making semantic connections deepens word knowledge. Varying the contexts (song titles, top ten weekend activities for a leopard!) for the activity encourages creativity with language, too.

'that' before a singular or uncountable masculine noun
'that' before a singular or uncountable feminine noun
'those' before a plural masculine noun
'those' before a plural feminine noun

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: ‘Ese’, 'esa', 'aquel' and 'aquella' all mean 'that' before a singular or uncountable noun.
‘Esos’, 'esas', 'aquellos' and 'aquellas' all mean 'those' before a plural noun.
'Aquel', 'aquella', 'aquellos' and 'aquellas' refer to something far away in space or time.
Spanish demonstrative adjectives agree in gender with the noun.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: 'Aquel' and 'aquella' also mean 'that' and refer to something far away in space or time.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: 'Ese' and 'esa' are the only words for 'that' before a noun in Spanish.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the demonstrative adjectives 'aquel', 'aquella', 'aquellos' and 'aquellas' to refer to things in a clothes shop.

teacherTips.teacherTip: 'Aquel', 'aquella', 'aquellos' and 'aquellas' are all Higher-tier grammar features.

lessons.lessonTitle: De compras: demonstrative pronoun 'aquello'
lessons.unitTitle: Lifestyle and wellbeing: de compras

lessonKeywords.description: specifies a particular noun, indicating 'this', 'that', 'these' or 'those'
replaces the noun, indicating 'this (one)', 'that (one)', 'these (ones)' or 'those (ones)'
demonstrative pronoun meaning ‘that (thing)'
part of the verb that appears in all forms

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: 'Aquel' and 'aquella' both mean 'that' before a singular or uncountable noun.
'Aquello' means 'that (thing)' for something that is unspecified.
'Aquello' never appears before a noun and often appears before the relative pronoun 'que'.
Verbs like 'poner' add 'g' to the end of the stem in the first person singular of the present tense.
Verbs like 'conocer' add 'z' before the final 'c' of the stem in the first person singular of the present tense.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The letter 'g' replaces the 'c' in hacer in the first person singular of the present tense.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The verb 'hacer' follows the same rule as 'poner' for forming the 1st person singular of the present tense.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the demonstrative pronoun 'aquello' and verbs like 'conocer' and 'poner' in the context of a clothes shop.

teacherTips.teacherTip: 'Aquello' is an example of a Higher-tier grammar feature. A1 option 1 practises new vocabulary, while option 2 practises revisited vocabulary.

lessons.lessonTitle: De compras: conversation practice, role-play
lessons.unitTitle: Lifestyle and wellbeing: de compras

lessonKeywords.description: form of pronouns and verbs used to refer to 'she', 'he', 'it', 'they', or 'you (formal)'
word that connects ideas between clauses in a sentence
word or short phrase that connects ideas between sentences

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: When preparing and performing role-plays, it’s important to include a verb in each answer.
Questions in some role-plays may be addressed to 'usted' and therefore use language in the third person singular.
Opinions about shopping can be developed by giving justifications and contrasts.
Conjunctions can provide justifications and connectives can provide contrasts.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In a role-play pupils need to answer each question with a short phrase or sentence.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: It is sufficient to give one-word answers in a role-play.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can perform a role-play in a shop and answer questions about shopping.

teacherTips.teacherTip: It can be useful to repeat the role-play in order to build fluency and reduce reliance on notes. Note that it is only in Edexcel role-plays that the pupil may be addressed as 'usted'.

lessons.lessonTitle: ¡Qué emocionante! 'Ser' and 'estar' present

In Spanish, there are two ways to say ‘to be’. Use ser with permanent traits and estar with location, states and moods.
Extended reading texts can be exploited to enrich our thematic vocabulary and use of complex structures.
It is important to communicate accurately but also to include varied and complex language.
It is helpful to reference popular customs and celebrations in different Hispanic countries in this topic.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: 'She, he is doing' is 'está haciendo'. To form the present continuous, use 'estar' and a verb in the present participle (-ando, -iendo).
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: 'She, he is doing' translates as 'es haciendo' in Spanish.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use a variety of vocabulary and structures to talk about a festival in the Hispanic world.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Support can be provided through the model text included in Task C1. Encourage students to use this as a model. This is also a great opportunitiy to encourage students to  curate their own topic-spcific vocabulary and structures related to the festivals they find more interesting.

lessons.lessonTitle: El día de Muertos: 'estar' + present participle, adverbs of position

[ll] and [y] are pronounced the same. [ll] sounds like 'llevar' and [y] sounds like 'ayuda'.
The singular present tense forms of 'estar' are 'estoy', 'estás, 'está'.
'Estar' + present participle of -ar and -er/-ir verbs (-ando, -iendo) is used to talk about ongoing events.
Verbs whose stems end in a vowel ('leer', 'construir') have an i->y spelling change for the present participle ending.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Verbs whose stems end in a vowel ('leer', 'construir') have a i->y spelling change when in the past participle ending.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All present participles follow regular rules and there are no spelling exceptions.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use singular persons of 'estar' to talk about where I and others are and what I and others are doing at a festival.

lessons.lessonTitle: Los Sanfermines: affirmative imperative (-e), possessive adjectives

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: 'Me' means 'to me' and 'my', and 'te' means 'to you' and 'your'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the imperative to give advice and instructions about what to do at a festival.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Teachers might want to allocate time for students to research one of the festivals included in Task D3. lessons.lessonTitle: Las peñas (los clubs) de los pueblos: 'estar' + present participle

'Estar' in present tense, plural persons has the forms 'estamos', 'estáis' and 'están'.
Estar + present participle of -ar & -er / -ir (-ando, -iendo) is used to talk about ongoing events.
Peñas are associations of people who gather together to celebrate local costumes and traditions.
When describing a photo include description of: people, action, location and mood.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: You are (singular) and you are (plural) are translated the same in Spanish - 'estás'.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The last-syllable stress rule is aimed at Higher students and there is a choice of tasks in the second learning cycle to reflect this. Task B1 Option 1 is F/H whereas task B1 Option 2 and the appropriate check tests Higher-only phonological knowledge: application of the last-syllable stress rule.

When talking to somebody familiar to you (tú) with the affirmative imperative with -ar verbs, use the ending -a.

La Tomatina is a Spanish festival in Buñol, where participants throw tomatoes at each other.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the imperative to tell somebody what to do at a famous Spanish festival, la Tomatina.

teacherTips.teacherTip: As an extended and creative writing task, teachers can ask students to write their own 'rules' and advice for the festival. It's important to remind them to use the affirmative imperative and stay away from giving negative commands as this triggers the subjunctive.

We can use the simple present and the present continuous when making plans with friends.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the simple present and present continuous to make plans to meet up with friends.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Teachers can adapt task C4b by giving pupils the freedom to choose the content of their dialogue. They can provide bullets in English with a brief description on what kind of information to include (time to meet up, place, what they are doing, etc.).

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The [z] sound is pronounced as in 'bath' or 'thorn'.
To use negation in Spanish, 'no' is widely used.
To make a verb negative, 'no' is placed before the verb.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The sound [z] is pronounced differently in parts of Spain and in other parts of the world.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The sound [z] is pronounced the same in every Spanish-speaking country.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use 'no' to ask and answer about what I do and don’t do in school.

lessons.lessonTitle: Free time: -er and -ir verbs 2nd person singular in questions
lessons.unitTitle: Activities in and out of school: -er and -ir verbs

lessonKeywords.description: describes habitual events in the present, e.g. 'you do'
describes completed events in the past, e.g. 'you did'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Words with stress on the third-last syllable have a written accent on the stressed vowel.
The 2nd person singular of -er and -ir verbs ends in -es in the present.
The 2nd person singular of -er and -ir verbs in ends in -iste in the preterite.
In Spanish we use 'de' between two nouns to describe a particular type of something.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In Spanish, the word order changes and the preposition 'de' is used between the two nouns, e.g. 'train ticket' is 'billete de tren'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: When in English there are two nouns together to describe a particular type of something, e.g. 'train ticket', in Spanish we translate them in the same order.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can ask and answer questions about free-time activities.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The teacher might want to follow activity B4 by a speaking activity where students move around the classroom and ask each other these questions.

lessons.lessonTitle: Free time: -er and -ir verbs 2nd person singular
lessons.unitTitle: Activities in and out of school: -er and -ir verbs

lessonKeywords.description: some words in Spanish have emphasis on the third-last syllable of a word when it is spoken
form of pronouns and verbs used to refer to yourself, i.e. 'I'
form of pronouns and verbs used to refer to who the speaker is adressing, i.e. 'you'
describes completed events in the past, e.g. 'I did'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Words with stress on the third-last syllable have an accent on the stressed vowel.
The 1st person singular of -er and -ir verbs ends in (-í) in the preterite.
The 2nd person singular of -er and -ir verbs ends in (-iste) in the preterite.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In Spanish 'pie' is also a 1-syllable word but we hear each letter distinctly, and Spanish 'i' is pronounced 'i' as in the Spanish word 'idea'. To say it correctly, enunciate each letter but quickly so that the word sounds as one syllable, 'p-i-e'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the preterite of -er and -ir verbs to talk about free time.

lessons.lessonTitle: At school: -er and -ir verbs 1st person singular preterite
lessons.unitTitle: Activities in and out of school: -er and -ir verbs

lessonKeywords.description: describes completed events in the past, e.g. 'I did'
describes habitual events in the present, e.g. 'I do'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: If the final syllable is stressed and the word ends in a vowel or 'n' or 's' there is an accent on the final vowel.
The 1st person singular of -er and -ir verbs in preterite ends in -í, e.g. 'describí'.
The 1st person singular of -er and -ir verbs in present ends in -o, e.g.' describo'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: -er and -ir verbs share the same endings in the preterite. The 'I' form of both -er and -ir verbs is -í.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: -er and -ir verbs have different endings in the preterite.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use -er/-ir verbs to talk about what I did and do at school.

lessons.lessonTitle: At school: prenominal adjectives
lessons.unitTitle: Activities in and out of school: -er and -ir verbs

lessonKeywords.description: adjectives that go before the noun

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: If the final syllable is stressed and the word ends in a vowel or 'n' or 's' there is an accent on the final vowel.
The 1st person singular of -er and -ir verbs in preterite ends in -í, e.g. 'elegí'.
The 1st person singular of -er and -ir verbs in present ends in -o, e.g.' elijo'.
Usually Spanish adjectives come after the noun, except for prenominal adjectives which come before the noun.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Most adjectives in Spanish go after the noun, except prenominal adjectives, which go before the noun. Some prenominal adjectives are: 'último', 'primero', 'segundo', 'tercero', 'bueno', 'propio'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All adjectives in Spanish go after the noun.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the correct position of adjectives when talking about activities at school.

lessonKeywords.description: describes habitual actions in the present, e.g. 'I play football'
words or phrases that tell you when something happens
form of pronouns and verbs used to refer to ‘she’, ‘he’, ‘it’, ‘they’

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: It is importantly to see words in context to effectively strengthen vocabulary.

Conversation answers can be developed using adverbs of time and 3rd person language.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: It is important to develop conversation answers to showcase a range of vocabulary and grammar. This can be achieved by using adverbs to add more detail and by incorporating a range of grammatical persons.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Conversation answers should be kept as short and simple as possible.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can talk on the topic of free time in the present tense using adverbs of time and a range of grammatical persons.

form of a verb used to form the perfect tense, e.g. 'listened', 'bought'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The perfect tense is used to express what has happened, e.g. 'I have listened', 'I have bought.
In Spanish, the perfect tense is formed from the auxiliary verb 'haber' and the past participle.
It is important to read the questions before the audio and listen the whole text before answering listening questions.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: It is important not to rush, and to listen to the whole text before answering a listening question.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: I should mark down the first thing I hear as the correct answer when answering listening questions.

lessons.unitTitle: Popular culture: el deporte

lessonKeywords.description: a letter or group of letters added to the end of a word to change its meaning or how it is used
suffix meaning ‘that can be …’ or ‘worthy of being …’
replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to, when the action is to me, for you, to them

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The suffix -able is used to form adjectives and it is typically added to -ar verbs.
Indirect object pronouns replace the person or thing that the action is done to, when it is to me, for you, to them.
Indirect object pronouns in Spanish are ‘me’, ‘te’, ‘le’ and ‘les’.
Indirect object pronouns precede the verb in 1-verb constructions, e.g. ‘me da la pelota’.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In 1-verb constructions, indirect object pronouns precede the verb in Spanish. This word order is different to English.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: As in English, indirect object pronouns follow the verb in Spanish.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the suffix -able and indirect object pronouns in the context of football and other sports.

lessons.lessonTitle: Órdenes para el equipo: plural affirmative commands
lessons.unitTitle: Popular culture: el deporte

lessonKeywords.description: form of verbs used to give instructions or commands

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Use the affirmative imperative to tell somebody to do something or to give instructions.
When talking to people familiar to you ('vosotros') with the affirmative imperative of an -ar verb, use the ending -ad.
When talking to people familiar to you ('vosotros') with the affirmative imperative of an -er verb, use the ending -ed.
When talking to people familiar to you ('vosotros') with the affirmative imperative of an -ir verb, use the ending -id.
The final -d of reflexive plural imperative verbs is dropped and -os is added, e.g. '¡callaos!' - 'be quiet!' (you pl).

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: To form the plural imperative of a reflexive verb, drop the final -d and add the pronoun -os to a plural imperative verb.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: To form the plural imperative of a reflexive verb, add the pronoun -os to a plural imperative verb.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use plural affirmative commands to give instructions to a sports team.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Learning Cycle 2 includes Higher-tier vocabulary. For Task B2b, make sure that the sentences from B2a are not visible so students don't copy the verbs.

lessons.lessonTitle: Órdenes del profe de deporte: singular affirmative commands
lessons.unitTitle: Popular culture: el deporte

lessonKeywords.description: form of verbs used to give instructions or commands

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Use the affirmative imperative to tell somebody to do something or to give instructions.
When talking to somebody familiar to you ('tú') with the affirmative imperative of an -ar verb, use the ending -a.
When talking to somebody familiar to you ('tú') with the affirmative imperative of an -er/-ir verb, use the ending -e.
Irregular imperative verbs include: 'sé', 've', 'ten', 'ven', 'haz', 'di', 'pon', 'sal'.
To form the familiar affirmative imperative of reflexive verbs, add the pronoun 'te' along with any necessary accents.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: When talking to somebody familiar to you ('tú') with the affirmative imperative of an -ar verb, use the ending -a, and for an -er or -ir verb, use the ending -e. Irregular imperative verbs include: 'sé', 've', 'ten', 'ven', 'haz', 'di', 'pon', 'sal'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: To give an order or command to 'tú' (you, informal), you should use the 2nd person singular form of the verb.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use singular affirmative commands in the context of a PE lesson.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Task B2 could be made into a competition whereby the first member of the class to complete the instruction wins the round.

lessons.lessonTitle: El fútbol: regular and irregular -er / -ir verbs
lessons.unitTitle: Popular culture: el deporte

lessonKeywords.description: spelling change in certain forms of a verb to preserve or aid pronunciation

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Some verb forms contain orthographic changes. These are spelling changes made to preserve or aid pronunciation.
Some -er / -ir verbs with ‘g’ in the stem change to 'j' in the 1st person singular to preserve the soft [g] sound.
Verbs ending in -uir gain a 'y' in persons 1,2,3 and 6 to aid pronunciation.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The verb 'influir' does not follow the normal pattern of -ir verbs. Verbs ending in -uir gain a 'y' in persons 1,2,3 and 6 to aid pronunciation. As such, the 1st person singular forms of 'influir' is 'influyo'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The 1st person singular form of 'influir' is 'influo'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can transcribe and conjugate a range of regular and irregular -er /-ir verbs in the context of football.

teacherTips.teacherTip: In Learning Cycle 1, slides 9-13 and Task A2 contain Higher Tier vocabulary. In Learning Cycle 2, verbs like 'influir' is a Higher Tier grammatical concept, but reference to these in the explanation and tasks could be easily removed for Foundation Tier students.

lessons.lessonTitle: Parejas famosas: possessive adjectives 'su' and 'sus' (his, her, their)
lessons.unitTitle: Media and technology: actores y películas

lessonKeywords.description: an adjective referring to possession; in English this includes 'my' and 'your'
a tense used for completed events in the past
a word in more than one language that has the same meaning and linguistic origin

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: To say ‘his’, ‘her’ or ‘its’ before a singular or uncountable noun, both masculine and singular, we use ‘su’.
‘Su’ and ‘sus’ mean ‘their’, referring to something that belongs to more than one person.
Spanish doesn’t have a word for ‘do’ or ‘did’ in questions (auxiliary). Only the main verb is used.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The final ‘s’ refers to a plural noun.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The final ‘-s’ in ‘sus’ refers to more than one person.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use ‘su’ and ‘sus’ with -ar verbs to ask questions about a famous Spanish-speaking couple.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Emphasise the importance of context in understanding the meaning of 'su'. This will help students to understand whether it means 'his', 'her', 'its' or 'their'.

lessons.lessonTitle: Dos actores famosos: -ar 3rd person singular and plural preterite
lessons.unitTitle: Media and technology: actores y películas

lessonKeywords.description: a tense used for events completed in the past
the verb as it appears in a dictionary
a type of pronoun that refers to a self-directed action; in English this includes the words ‘himself’ and ‘herself’

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Regular -ar verbs: 3rd person singular and plural, PAST preterite (-ó, -aron).
The sound [j] followed by any vowel sounds like 'jugar'.
The sound [g] followed by a, o or u sounds like 'gol'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The reflexive pronoun 'se' appears before a conjugated verb in any tense.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Reflexive pronouns appear after a conjugated verb.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can write about a famous Spanish-speaking couple by using -ar verbs in the past (preterite) tense.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Allow plenty of time for students to complete the final writing activity. Students may also benefit from receiving feedback on their translation of the first paragraph before moving on to the second.

lessons.lessonTitle: Artistas conocidos: possessive adjective 'vuestro'
lessons.unitTitle: Media and technology: actores y películas

lessonKeywords.description: an adjective referring to possession; in English, this includes 'my' and 'your'
a tense used for completed events in the past
Spanish word meaning 'your' for two or more people; feminine singular and plural forms are 'vuestra', 'vuestros', 'vuestras'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: It is important to distinguish between the [j] + vowel and [g] + a, o or u sounds.
To say 'your' for two or more people, use 'vuestro'.
'Vuestro' is used for a singular or uncountable masculine noun and 'vuestros' is used for a plural masculine noun.
'Vuestra' is used for a singular or uncountable feminine noun and 'vuestras' is used for a plural feminine noun.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: 'Tu' means 'your' when addressing one person. 'Vuestro' means 'your' when addressing more than one person.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: There is only one word for 'your' in Spanish.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use possessive adjectives and -ar verbs to describe the lives of two Spanish-speaking artists.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The Option 2 version of Task C1 in Cycle 3 provides the noun genders in brackets for pupils who need a little more support. The final writing activity brings together a range of language from the unit. It may be useful to recap the reflexive pronoun 'se' before beginning this.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: A diphthong is created when a strong vowel appears next to a weak vowel, making a single syllable.
To mean ‘you (all) are’ for location, state or mood, use ‘estáis’.
To mean ‘you (all) are’ for general traits, use ‘sois’.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In Spanish, the verb 'ser' means 'to be, being' for general traits. To refer to a location, mood or state, use 'estar'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: In Spanish, I can use the verb 'ser' to talk about 'being' in any context.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use ‘estáis’ and ‘sois’ to describe moods, states and general traits in the context of sport and health.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The worksheet for this lesson is necessary for Task B1. You could add some pictures of the basketball teams mentioned in Task C1 to enhance the cultural content of the lesson.

lessons.lessonTitle: Health: 'vuestro' and 'vuestra'

lessonKeywords.description: word that goes before a noun to show ownership or belonging e.g. ‘your’
'your’ for one person before a singular noun
'your’ for more than one person before a masculine singular noun
‘your’ for more than one person before a feminine singular noun

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: To mean ‘your’ for one person before a singular noun, use ‘tu’.
To mean ‘your’ for more than one person before a masculine singular noun, use ‘vuestro’.
To mean ‘your’ for more than one person before a feminine singular noun, use ‘vuestra’.
To form 2nd person singular -ar verbs in the present tense, use the verb ending -as.
To form 2nd person plural -ar verbs in the present tense, use the verb ending -áis.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Saying 'your' in Spanish depends on the number of people you are speaking to and the following noun. To mean ‘your’ for one person before a singular noun, use ‘tu’, and for more than one person, use 'vuestro' or 'vuestra'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: As in English, there is one way of saying 'your' in Spanish.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the possessive adjectives ‘tu’ and ‘vuestro’ and ‘vuestra’ in the context of health.

teacherTips.teacherTip: If greater scaffolding is required for Task C2, you could play the audio twice to allow students to focus on one thing at once. The first time round students would select the correct word and the second time they would write the action.

lessons.lessonTitle: Sport and exercise: -ar verbs 2nd person singular and plural
lessons.unitTitle: Sport and healthy living: present continuous, 'vuestro/a'

lessonKeywords.description: form of pronouns and verbs used to refer to 'you' (one person)
form of pronouns and verbs used to refer to 'you' (several people)

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: 2nd person verbs refer to 'you' (singular or plural).
To form 2nd person singular -ar verbs in the present tense, use the verb ending -as.
To form 2nd person plural -ar verbs in the present tense, use the verb ending -áis.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: To conjugate 2nd person plural -ar verbs, use the verb ending -áis. The accent on the 'a' is important as it tells us to stress the final syllable.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: To conjugate 2nd person plural -ar verbs, use the verb ending -ais.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can discuss sport and exercise using singular and plural 2nd person verbs.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You could set a time limit for Task B1 to create a sense of urgency and competition.

lessons.lessonTitle: Sport and exercise: present continuous with -AR verbs
