lessonKeywords.description: sound formed by the combination of two vowels in one syllable
describes events happening right now, e.g. 'I am playing'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: A diphthong is a sound formed by the combination of two vowels in one syllable.
To say you (sg) are doing something with an -ar verb, use 'estás' + a verb ending in -ando.
To say you (pl) are doing something with an -ar verb, use 'estáis' + a verb ending in -ando.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In Spanish, there are different verb endings to refer to 'you' (singular) and 'you' (plural). For -ar verbs these are -as and -áis.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Like in English, I can use the same form of the verb to adress 'you' for one person and 'you' for several people.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use 2nd person singular and plural forms of the present continuous in the context of a PE lesson.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You could show students a video of a 'pelota vasca' game to highlight the fast pace of the sport.

lessons.lessonTitle: Weekend activities: pronouns 'me', 'te', 'le', 'se' and 'les'
lessons.unitTitle: Weekends: 'ser', 'estar', 'ir' and 'hacer'

lessonKeywords.description: reflexive pronoun 'himself', 'herself' or 'itself'
used to indicate doing something to yourself, words like 'myself' and 'yourself'
replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to, when the action is to me, for you, to them

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: When the 'doer' (subject) and 'receiver' (object) of an action are the same person we use a reflexive pronoun.
To mean 'herself' or 'himself' in Spanish, use 'se' before a verb.
Indirect object pronouns (e.g. 'him', 'them') indicate the person or thing that is indirectly affected by the verb.
If the person affected by the action is 'me', use 'me'; if the person affected by the action is 'you', use 'te'.
To refer to one person or thing indirectly affected by an action use 'le', for more than one person or thing use 'les'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: 'Le' means 'to him', 'to her' or 'to it' regardless of the person receiving the action, e.g. 'le doy un regalo a Lucía' or 'le doy un regalo a Daniel'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The indirect object pronoun 'le' changes to 'la' to match the gender of the person receiving the action.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can distinguish between actions done to others and to oneself using the reflexive pronoun 'se', and I can use indirect object pronouns to talk about weekend activities.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This lesson receptively revisits two different types of pronouns that pupils have previously learned. Teachers will know for their classes if they want to focus instead on just one of these, and add in a productive practice task for it.

lessons.lessonTitle: A trip to Asturias: 'ser' and 'estar' 1st and 3rd person
lessons.unitTitle: Weekends: 'ser', 'estar', 'ir' and 'hacer'

lessonKeywords.description: verb 'to be, being' used to describe permanent traits
verb 'to be, being' used to describe temporary state/mood and location
form of an adjective or adverb used to used to compare people, things or ideas
conjunction used in comparative structures meaning 'than'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: In Spanish there are two verbs for 'to be'. Use 'estar' for location, state or mood and 'ser' for permanent traits.
Some adjectives can only be used with ‘estar’ because they only describe a state, not a permanent trait.
The 1st person singular of 'estar' is 'estoy' and the plural is 'estamos'; for 'ser', it is 'soy' and 'somos'.
The 3rd person singular of 'estar' is 'está', and the plural is 'están'; for 'ser', it is 'es' and 'son'.
To say 'more … than' in Spanish, use 'más' + adjective + 'que'; to say 'less … than', use 'menos' + adjective + 'que'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The verb 'ser' is for permanent traits, and the verb 'estar' is for temporary states/moods and location. It sounds as odd to a Spanish person if we use the wrong verb 'to be' as it does when someone says 'I make sport' or 'I do a cake' in English.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: It doesn't matter which Spanish translation of the verb 'to be' we use, as they both mean 'to be, being'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the 1st and 3rd person forms of 'ser' and 'estar', as well as comparative structures, to describe a trip to Asturias.

teacherTips.teacherTip: To develop Task C1, teachers can encourage students to identify all the comparative structures and follow up by asking them to create their own comparative sentences, using the 1st and 3rd person forms of 'ser' and 'estar'.

lessons.lessonTitle: Weekend activities: -ar verbs 2nd person singular and plural
lessons.unitTitle: Weekends: 'ser', 'estar', 'ir' and 'hacer'

lessonKeywords.description: form of pronouns and verbs used to refer to 'you' and 'you all'
verb form that forms the present continuous, together with the auxiliary verb 'estar'
replaces the noun receiving the action of the verb, e.g. 'me', 'you', 'it', 'them'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: When strong vowels [a], [e] and [o] appear next to each other they are pronounced separately, in different syllables.
The second person singular of 'estar' is ‘estás’ and the 2nd person plural is ‘estáis’.
We use the present continuous to express an ongoing event. It is formed by using 'estar' + the present participle.
To mean ‘them’ when referring to a plural feminine object, use the direct object pronoun 'las' before a verb.
To mean ‘them’ for a plural masculine object, use the direct object pronoun 'los' before a verb.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: 'Los' and 'las' mean 'the' in front of a plural noun but 'them' when they come before a verb.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: 'Los' and 'las' always mean 'the'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use -ar verbs in the 2nd person to talk about what is happening now and correctly use the direct object pronouns 'los' and 'las' to describe weekend activities.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Teachers can make use of transitional moments during lessons to encourage pupils to use the present continuous. The questions '¿Qué estás haciendo?' and '¿Qué estáis haciendo?', when asked with a touch of humour, are very effective and can be used repeatedly in the language classroom.

lessons.lessonTitle: Simon Bolívar y Manuela Sáenz: preterite irregular stems, relative clauses
lessons.unitTitle: Travel and tourism: Figuras históricas

lessonKeywords.description: adds information about the noun in the main clause
pronoun that introduces a relative clause
relative pronoun meaning 'who', 'that' or 'which'
relative pronoun meaning 'when'
relative pronoun meaning 'where'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: 'Decir', 'estar', 'venir', 'poner', 'querer', 'saber', 'traer' and 'poder' have irregular stems in the preterite.
Relative pronouns are words that introduce a relative clause, giving more information about a noun.
The relative pronoun 'que' means 'who, that, which', 'donde' means 'where' and 'cuando' means 'when'.
Unlike question words, relative pronouns in Spanish do not have a written accent.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: These relative pronouns do not have an accent, unlike the question words 'qué' ('who'), 'dónde' ('where') and 'cuándo' ('when').
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The relative pronouns 'que', 'donde' and 'cuando' have an accent.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can understand irregular verbs in the preterite tense and relative pronouns in the context of historical figures.

teacherTips.teacherTip: All grammar features in this lesson are part of the GCSE subject content at both Foundation and Higher tier.

lessons.lessonTitle: Una persona que me influye: relative pronoun ‘lo que’, extended writing
lessons.unitTitle: Travel and tourism: Figuras históricas

lessonKeywords.description: a pronoun that introduces a relative clause
relative pronoun meaning 'what' or 'the thing that'
relative pronoun meaning 'who', 'that', 'which' or 'the person who'
acronym for extended writing

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The relative pronoun 'lo que' means 'what' or 'the thing that' and refers to a general idea.
The relative pronoun 'lo que' can be used to extend written answers.
When translating into English, it is important to identify who or what the relative pronoun refers to.
When translating into English, it is important to consider the position of the prepositions within a sentence.
Use the acronym BORDER to structure, develop and enhance your response with key content and varied language.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: 'Lo que' means 'what' or 'the thing that'. It refers to a general idea, rather than a specific noun or person.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: 'Lo que' can refer to a specific noun or a person.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the relative pronoun 'lo que' to extend a piece of writing about an influential person.

teacherTips.teacherTip: 'Lo que' is a Higher-tier grammar feature. Task D1 presents a good opportunity for peer marking; you could encourage students to swap books and check for each part of BORDER in each other's answers.

lessons.lessonTitle: Un revolucionario: relative pronouns 'el que' and 'el cual'
lessons.unitTitle: Travel and tourism: Figuras históricas

lessonKeywords.description: pronoun that introduces a relative clause
relative pronoun meaning 'that', 'which' or 'who' for a singular or uncountable noun
relative pronoun meaning 'that', 'which' or 'who' for a plural noun
relative pronoun meaning 'that', 'which' or 'who' for a singular or uncountable noun
relative pronoun meaning 'that', 'which' or 'who' for a plural noun

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: 'El que', 'la que', 'los que' and 'las que' mean 'that', 'which' or 'who' and often appear after a preposition.
'El que', 'la que', 'los que' and 'las que' agree in gender and number with the noun.
'El cual', 'la cual', 'los cuales' and 'las cuales' mean 'that', 'which' or 'who' and often appear after a preposition.
'El cual', 'la cual', 'los cuales' and 'las cuales' agree in gender and number with the noun.
'El cual' tends to appear in more formal contexts than 'el que'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: 'El cual' tends to appear in more formal contexts than 'el que'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: 'El que' and 'el cual' are completely interchangeable.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the relative pronouns 'el que' and 'el cual' in the context of describing a revolutionary figure.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The relative pronouns 'el que' and 'el cual' (and their inflected forms) are Higher-tier grammar features.

lessons.lessonTitle: How people feel: idiomatic uses of 'tener' + noun
lessons.unitTitle: Describing how people feel: 'tener' and 'dar' + noun

lessonKeywords.description: -er verb meaning 'to have, having'; with some nouns 'tener' also translates as 'to be, being'
a phrase or expression whose meaning we don't translate word-for-word, e.g. 'it's raining cats and dogs'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The verb 'tener' can also be translated as 'to be + adjective' when used as an idiom, 'tener + noun'.
Its singular forms are: 'tengo', 'tienes', 'tiene' and its plural forms are: 'tenemos' and 'tienen'.
The Spanish plural subject pronouns are: 'nosotros/as', 'ellos/as'. They add clarity about who the verb refers to.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The verb 'tener' translates into English as 'to be' when used as part of idioms, e.g. 'tengo suerte' translates as 'I am lucky'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The verb 'tener' always means 'to have, having'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the verb 'tener' to describe how people feel.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The teacher might want to add an element of competition by doing activity B5 as a paired activity where the first pair to translate the sentences are the winners.

lessons.lessonTitle: What people have: 'tener' singular persons
lessons.unitTitle: Describing how people feel: 'tener' and 'dar' + noun

lessonKeywords.description: -er verb meaning 'to have, having'
represents the person, people or thing(s) doing the verb, e.g. 'I', 'we, 'they'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The SSCs [ca], [co] and [cu] are pronounced as in 'casa', 'comer', 'escuchar'.
The verb 'tener' means 'to have, having' and we use it to talk about possessions.
The singular persons of 'tener' are 'tengo' ('I have'), 'tienes' ('you have') and 'tiene' ('she, he, it has').
The Spanish singular subject pronouns are: 'yo', 'tú', 'él', 'ella'.
We need numbers to talk about plural possessions; such sentences often contain 'tener', numbers and plural nouns.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Numbers 16 to 19 begin with 'dieci-' + number, e.g. 'dieciséis', 'diecisiete', but numbers 13 to 15 do not follow the same pattern, e.g. 'trece', 'catorce', 'quince'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All numbers from 13 to 19 begin with 'dieci-'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the verb ‘tener’ to talk about what I and others have.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The teacher might want to play a class bingo using the numbers learned today.

lessons.lessonTitle: Free time: what people do
lessons.unitTitle: Describing how people feel: 'tener' and 'dar' + noun

lessonKeywords.description: a letter or group of letters added to the end of a word to change its meaning or how it is used, e.g. 'educate' → 'education'
a verb that does not follow the regular rules
-ar irregular verb meaning 'to give, giving'
-er irregular verb meaning 'to want, wanting'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The suffix '-tion' at the end of an English word is often '-ción' in Spanish; all '-ción' words are feminine.
'-ción' words lose the accent in the plural form; this is because the stress now falls on the penultimate syllable.
The verb 'dar' means 'to give, giving'; its plural 'we' form is 'damos'.
The verb 'querer' means 'to want, wanting'; its plural 'we' form is 'queremos'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: If a word ends in 'n' or 's' and has final syllable stress, it must have an accent, e.g. 'la opción'. However, if a word ending in 'n' or 's' has penultimate syllable stress, it does not need an accent, e.g. 'las opciones'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All the words ending in '-ción' and '-ciones' must have an accent.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can talk about what I and others do together in their free time using the irregular verbs 'dar' and 'querer'.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The teacher might want to ask students to create their own flashcards, so that they can use them to revise the vocabulary little and often.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The verb 'dar' means 'to give, giving' but can also translate as 'to be' + adjective when describing how something makes people feel.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The verb 'dar' always translates as 'to give, giving'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the irregular verb 'dar' to say how something makes people feel.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The teacher might want to show the words one-by-one in A1.

lessons.lessonTitle: Barcelona: plural definite articles 'los' and 'las'

lessonKeywords.description: pronounced as in 'ojo'
the words 'los' and 'las', meaning 'the'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: [j] is pronounced as in 'ojo'.
The plural definite article in Spanish is 'los' for masculine nouns and 'las' for feminine nouns.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In Spanish, the plural 'the' has two forms: 'los' for plural masculine nouns, and 'las' for plural feminine nouns.

lessons.lessonTitle: Castellón: write about where you live

lessonKeywords.description: the words 'el', 'la', 'los' and 'las', meaning 'the'
the words 'un', 'una', 'unos', 'unas', meaning 'a/an' and 'some'
when the ending of an adjective matches the noun it describes in gender and number

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The definite article in Spanish is 'el' and los' with masculine nouns and 'la' and 'las' with feminine nouns.
When using 'es', we need to use the singular form of the adjective.
When using 'son', we need to use the plural form of the adjective.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In Spanish, adjectives must agree with the noun they describe in gender and number. If the noun is feminine, the adjective will end in -a, but if it is masculine, it will end in -o. If the adjective already ends in -e, it will stay the same.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: In Spanish, adjectives always end in -o.

lessons.lessonTitle: What is there? What is it like? Singular definite and indefinite articles

lessonKeywords.description: pronounced as in 'gente'
pronounced as in 'imaginar'
the word 'a, an' that comes before a noun when it is mentioned for the first time
the word 'the' comes before a noun when it has been mentioned before in a sentence

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The SSC [ge] sounds like in 'gente'
The SSC [gi] sounds like in 'imaginar'
The indefinite article is used to introduce a noun and the definite article to refer to it again

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Both sounds are pronounced like an 'h' followed by 'e' for [ge] and followed by 'i' for [gi]
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The sounds [ge] and [gi] are pronounced just like in English.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the singular definite and the indefinite article to describe places in town.

lessons.lessonTitle: Describe cities: 'ser' 3rd person plural 'son'

lessonKeywords.description: pronounced as in 'ganar' like a hard 'g'
pronounced as in 'gol' like a hard 'g'
pronounced as in 'preguntar' like a hard 'g'
part of the verb 'ser' that means 'she, he, it is'
part of the verb 'ser' that means 'they are'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Sound-symbol correspondences [ga], [go], [gu] can be practised by pronouncing words like 'ganar', 'gol' and 'preguntar'.
'Es' means 'it is' to describe someone or something.
'Son' means 'they are' to describe two or more people or things.
Sentences with ‘hay’ usually begin with ‘en’. ‘Hay un(a)’ means ‘there is a/an’. ‘Hay unos/unas’ means ‘there are some.’
'Tiene' means 'she, he, it has'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: 'Es' means 'she, he, it is' and 'son' means 'they are'.

lessons.lessonTitle: Construir un futuro mejor: subjunctive after wishing

lessonKeywords.description: verb form that indicates actions which are uncertain, wished for, or that have not yet happened
expresses a desire, hope or preference for something to happen; these verbs often introduce the subjunctive after 'que'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The subjunctive expresses uncertainty, wishes, emotions or future possibilities.
Use 'cuando' + indicative if the action is regular or certain, and 'cuando' + subjunctive if the action is uncertain.

Wishing verbs ('querer', 'esperar', 'desear', 'preferir', 'necesitar') are followed by an infinitive or the subjunctive.
Use a verb of wishing + 'que' + subjunctive when you want someone else to do something.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Use 'quiero' + infinitive when you want to do something yourself. Use 'quiero' + 'que' + subjunctive when you want someone else to do something. Both forms often talk about the future, but the change of subject triggers the use of subjunctive.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: 'Quiero', espero', 'deseo', 'prefiero' are always followed by infinitives.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The subjunctive expresses uncertainty, wishes, emotions or future possibilities.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The inflectional future tense is used to express what will happen.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: 'Cuando' is always followed by the subjunctive.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: This is only the case with attribute verbs like 'ser' or 'estar' because the adjective is still referring to an implicit noun (person, thing).

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: This is one of the rare cases in Spanish where one sound can have two spellings.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can  read aloud and understand a Spanish poem.

Plural adjectives ending in -es do not change for gender.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: This is the general case, but it is not a rule. There are many cases where the adjective precedes the noun, like for certain collocations ('una gran amistad') or when more flair is sought.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Spanish adjectives always follow the noun.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use plural adjectives to describe places in the Spanish-speaking world.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: ‘Hay’ or ‘tiene’ with an indefinite article introduces a noun.
A definite article often refers back to a previously introduced noun.
To express what someone wants, use ‘querer’, and to give something, use ‘dar’.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Some nouns are uncountable and have no plural. Use these without an article, as in English. For example, 'quiere dinero' means 'she, he wants money'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All nouns in Spanish are always used with an article, a word for 'a', 'some' or 'the'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use ‘dar’, ‘querer’ and other language I know to adapt a poem in my speaking and writing.

verb meaning 'we have'

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The [r] and [rr] sounds need practice to produce them confidently. Even for native speakers, it is the last sound that children learn to produce.

lessons.lessonTitle: Guernica - una obra de arte única: indefinite adjectives and pronouns

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist and key 20th-century figure, known for co-pioneering the Cubist movement.
'Guernica' is Picasso's famous anti-war painting, showing the horror of the Spanish Civil War bombing in 1937.
'Alguno/a' and 'algunos/as' mean 'some', 'any' or 'a', 'an' and are used in affirmative sentences and questions.
'Ninguno' and 'ninguna' mean 'none', 'no-one', 'not a single one'; they are always used in the singular form.
Indefinite adjectives and indefinite pronouns are identical apart from the masculine singular form.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: 'Ningún' and 'ninguno' look very similar but they are used differently in Spanish. 'Ninguno' is a pronoun and it replaces a masculine singular noun. 'Ningún' is an indefinite adjective and it comes before a masculine singular noun.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: There is no difference between 'ningún' and 'ninguno'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use indefinite adjectives and indefinite pronouns to describe the painting 'Guernica'.

teacherTips.teacherTip: After exploring the painting 'Guernica' in this lesson, teachers might suggest that pupils find out more about the Spanish Civil War, e.g. on BBC Bitesize.

lessons.lessonTitle: En países donde se habla español: -ar present tense 2nd persons

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Spanish is the official language in 21 countries across 3 different continents.

In Latin America, 'ustedes' is used for both formal and informal situations instead of 'vosotros'.
The ending for 2nd person singular for -ar verbs in the present tense is -as and -áis for the 2nd person plural.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Spanish is the official language in 21 countries across 3 different continents.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can understand information about lifestyles across different Spanish-speaking countries.

teacherTips.teacherTip: After the lesson on Spanish-speaking countries and language variations, teachers can direct students to search for 'BBC Languages - A Guide to Spanish'. Ask students to choose one interesting fact about Spanish from the website and present it to the class.

lessons.lessonTitle: ¿Adónde fuiste? Extended writing

lessonKeywords.description: acronym used to respond fully and accurately to bullet point writing prompts
a proofreading technique to improve the accuracy of verbs, adjectives and nouns

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The BORDER acronym is a useful tool to respond fully and accurately to bullet point writing prompts.
The VAN check involves checking your verbs, adjectives and nouns after writing.
The VAN check can significantly improve accuracy when completing writing tasks.
You must respond to the bullet point using the correct tense (e.g. past, present, future) to fully address it.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: You must respond to the bullet point using the correct tense (e.g. past, present, future) to fully address it. Other tenses can add depth, but they don't replace the need to respond directly in the specified tense.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: As long as I say something about the topic, it doesn't matter what tense I use.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can produce a detailed piece of writing that uses the correct tense to respond directly to each bullet point.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Task B1 presents a good opportunity for peer marking; you could encourage students to swap books and check for each part of BORDER in each other's answers as well as use the VAN check.

lessons.lessonTitle: ¿Qué hay que ver? Impersonal uses of verbs
lessons.unitTitle: Travel and tourism: lugares y personas famosos

lessonKeywords.description: 3rd person form of a verb that doesn’t refer to a specific person and is used without a subject
form of the verb giving its general meaning, with no subject or tense

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Andalusia (Andalucía in Spanish) is a region in southern Spain known for its rich history and culture.
To express opinions and make suggestions, we can use some impersonal verbs in the 3rd person singular.
Examples of impersonal uses of verbs are ‘basta (con)’, ‘falta’, ‘hace falta’, ‘parece’ and ‘vale la pena’ .
These impersonal verbs are used without a subject and followed by an infinitive.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Verbs like 'basta' and 'hace falta' can’t always be translated word-for-word - they don’t work the same way as English verbs. You need to choose the most idiomatic or natural-sounding translation based on the context.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: I can translate verbs like 'basta' and 'hace falta' word-for-word.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can make suggestions and express opinions about what to see and do in Spain using impersonal verbs.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Learning Cycle 2 contains Higher-tier grammar. Task B3 Option 1 has Higher-tier structures and vocabulary. Option 2 is for Foundation tier. The teacher uses Option 1 in both cases in the video. The Option 2 slides, audio and worksheets are available as required.

lessons.lessonTitle: Pequeños grandes cambios: perfect and present tenses
lessons.unitTitle: Travel and tourism: lugares y personas famosos

lessonKeywords.description: tense used to express what has happened, e.g. 'I have listened', 'I have bought'
special verb that helps form the perfect tense in Spanish, translated as 'have, has' in English, e.g. 'I have lived', 'he has spoken'
verb that helps form part of a 2-verb tense structure
form of a verb used to form the perfect tense, e.g. 'listened', 'bought'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The perfect tense is used to express what has happened.
To conjugate the perfect tense, use 'he', 'has', 'ha', 'hemos', 'habéis' or 'han' (from 'haber') + past participle.
To form the past participle of regular verbs, remove the -ar/-er/-ar and add -ado (-ar verbs) or -ido (-er/-ir verbs).
Remember to use the correct ending to refer to the right person in the present tense.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Although most Spanish past participles do follow these regular patterns, some verbs have irregular past participles which just need to be learnt, e.g. 'escrito' ('written'), 'visto' ('seen'), 'hecho' ('done'), 'dicho' ('said').
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All past participles in Spanish end in -ado (-ar verbs) or -ido (-er/-ir verbs).

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the present and perfect tenses to talk about small changes that have a big impact on our lives.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Teachers can end this lesson with a gratitude and micro-habit reflection exercise using sentence stems that clearly distinguish the tenses, e.g. 'Hoy estoy agradecido/a por/porque' and 'Cada día' + verb in the present tense.

lessons.lessonTitle: Buenas intenciones: subjunctive after 'para que'

lessonKeywords.description: verb form that indicates actions which are uncertain, wished for, or that have not yet happened; its forms are different from the indicative
preposition meaning 'to', 'for' + noun or 'in order to' + infinitive
conjunction meaning 'so that', which is followed by a subjunctive verb

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The subjunctive indicates uncertainty, wishing or possibility, or refers to actions that have not yet happened.
The conjunction 'para que' translates as 'so that' and is followed by a subjunctive verb.
Spanish uses the subjunctive after 'para que' even though English uses the indicative after 'so that'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: We only use 'para que' + subjunctive to express intentions when the subject of the 2nd verb in the sentence is different from the first. Where the subject is the same in the whole sentence, express intentions with 'para' + infinitive.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: We always use 'para que' + subjunctive to express intentions in Spanish.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the subjunctive after 'para que' to express purpose or intention.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Teachers can increase the level of challenge for Task B2 by asking students to translate the sentence without referring to the hints on the slide. Additionally, an extension could involve asking students to write their own sentence(s) with 'para' and/or 'para que'.

lessons.lessonTitle: Una visita especial: translation, transcription

lessonKeywords.description: process of listening to spoken words and writing them down accurately, also known as dictation
changing words or sentences from one language into another, so the meaning stays the same
a proofreading technique to improve the accuracy of verbs, adjectives, and nouns

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Successful transcription involves careful listening, writing and checking, ensuring every word written makes sense.
Effective translation requires more than direct word-for-word substitution.
The VAN check involves checking your verbs, adjectives and nouns after translating.
The VAN check can significantly improve accuracy when tackling translation tasks.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Effective translation requires more than direct word-for-word substitution. Applying knowledge of grammar and using proofing strategies, such as the VAN check (Verbs, Adjectives, Nouns), can significantly improve accuracy.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Translating word-for-word is an effective strategy when tackling translation tasks.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use different strategies to improve my dictation and translation skills.

teacherTips.teacherTip: In Learning Cycle 2, Option 1 in Task B1 has Higher-tier structures and vocabulary and Option 2 is for Foundation tier. Note that the Option 2 translation has been designed to revisit structures and vocabulary recently covered, rather than accurately represent an example translation.

lessons.lessonTitle: Lo mejor de todo: 'lo' + adjective
lessons.unitTitle: Travel and tourism: lugares y personas famosos

lessonKeywords.description: form of an adjective or adverb used to used to compare people, things or ideas
structure used to talk about general or abstract ideas, e.g. 'the best thing' or 'the bad part'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Grouping vocabulary thematically is an effective way to revise and retain words.
'Tan ... como' means 'as ... as' in comparisons.
To form other comparatives in Spanish, use 'más' or 'menos' + adjective + 'que'.
'Lo' + adjective is used to talk about general or abstract ideas, e.g. 'the best thing' or 'the bad part'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In Spanish, we use the structure 'lo' + adjective, so we do not include the word 'thing', e.g. 'lo mejor fue el final' translates into English as 'the best thing was the ending'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: I can translate 'the best thing was' word-for-word in Spanish.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can give my opinion using comparatives and 'lo' + adjective.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Despite the fact that the structure 'lo' + adjective is only examined at Higher Tier, it is a structure that many Foundation pupils will grasp, and enjoy adding to their spoken/written repertoire. As such, teachers may want to teach all of this lesson to their Foundation or mixed-tier groups.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use singular plural forms of 'ser' and 'ir' in the preterite tense in the context of a trip to a book fair.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Further consolidation of the misconception can be addressed in the lesson by asking students to translate the text in Task B2 during the final learning cycle.

lessonKeywords.description: acronym used to respond fully and accurately to bullet point writing prompts

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: When approaching extended writing tasks, dividing each bullet point into at least two paragraphs can be helpful.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: BORDER is also a very useful strategy for extended pieces of writing. Simply apply it to each paragraph separately. This will help you respond clearly and completely to each bullet point.

lessons.lessonTitle: Planes de viaje: photo description, conversation practice

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Manipulating present, past and future verbs allows you to tell a story and describe events clearly and accurately.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Whilst it is important to be able to refer to the future confidently, it is also helpful to add in different time frames to give more detail as well as opinions.

lessons.lessonTitle: El viaje de fin de curso: irregular verbs, uses of 'dar'
lessons.unitTitle: Travel and tourism: lugares y personas famosos

lessonKeywords.description: verb that does not follow the regular rules
-ar irregular verb meaning 'to give, giving'
replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to, when the action is to me, for you, to them

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Many of the most commonly-used Spanish verbs are irregular, e.g. 'ser', 'estar', 'tener', 'hacer', 'venir', 'dar', 'ir'.
The verb 'dar' can be used to describe how something makes people feel. English uses 'to be' + adjective for this.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The verb 'dar' means 'to give, giving' but can also translate as 'to be + adjective' when describing how something makes people feel.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The verb 'dar' always translates as 'to give, giving'.

lessons.lessonTitle: Vidas famosas - Frida Kahlo: indirect object pronouns in 2-verb structures

lessonKeywords.description: replaces the person(s) or thing(s) receiving the action of the verb, when the meaning is 'to' or 'for' someone

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Frida Kahlo was a Mexican painter known for her vivid self-portraits inspired by pain, identity, and Mexican culture.
Indirect object pronouns replace the person or thing that the action is done to when it is to me, for you, to them, etc.
Indirect object pronouns in Spanish are ‘me’, ‘te’, ‘le’ and ‘le', 'nos', 'os' and 'les'.
Indirect object pronouns can go before the conjugated verb or attach to the infinitive in two-verb constructions.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Spanish word order is different from English. Indirect object pronouns come before the conjugated verb. With 2-verb structures, they can go before the first verb or after the infinitive, attached to it.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Spanish word order is identical to English so I can translate sentences with indirect object pronouns literally from one language to another.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can understand and discuss key events and elements in Frida Kahlo’s life and artwork.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Students can deepen their understanding of Frida Kahlo's life and artistic expression by taking a virtual tour of La Casa Azul, her iconic Blue House in Mexico City, which can be accessed through the Frida Kahlo Museum's official website.

lessons.lessonTitle: Planes de viaje: subjunctive after verbs of emotion
lessons.unitTitle: Travel and tourism: lugares y personas famosos

lessonKeywords.description: verb form that indicates actions which are uncertain, wished for, or that have not yet happened; its forms are different from the indicative
expresses a feeling, emotional reaction, or psychological state; these verbs often introduce the subjunctive after 'que'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: In Spanish, to express a feeling, emotional reaction or opinion, you often use verbs of emotion.
Verbs of emotion ('gustar', 'encantar', 'dar', 'molestar', etc.) are followed by an infinitive or the subjunctive.
When verbs of emotion are followed by the conjunction 'que', use the subjunctive.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Spanish is the official language in 21 countries across 3 different continents.

In Latin America, 'ustedes' is used for both formal and informal situations instead of 'vosotros'.
The ending for 2nd person singular for -ar verbs in the present tense is -as and -áis for the 2nd person plural.

lessons.lessonTitle: ¿Qué hay que ver? Impersonal uses of verbs

To express opinions and make suggestions, we can use some impersonal verbs in the 3rd person singular.
Examples of impersonal uses of verbs are ‘basta (con)’, ‘falta’, ‘hace falta’, ‘parece’ and ‘vale la pena’ .
These impersonal verbs are used without a subject and followed by an infinitive.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Verbs like 'basta' and 'hace falta' can’t always be translated word-for-word - they don’t work the same way as English verbs. You need to choose the most idiomatic or natural-sounding translation based on the context.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: I can translate verbs like 'basta' and 'hace falta' word-for-word.

verb that helps form part of a 2-verb tense structure

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The perfect tense is used to express what has happened.
To conjugate the perfect tense, use 'he', 'has', 'ha', 'hemos', 'habéis' or 'han' (from 'haber') + past participle.
To form the past participle of regular verbs, remove the -ar/-er/-ar and add -ado (-ar verbs) or -ido (-er/-ir verbs).
Remember to use the correct ending to refer to the right person in the present tense.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Although most Spanish past participles do follow these regular patterns, some verbs have irregular past participles which just need to be learnt, e.g. 'escrito' ('written'), 'visto' ('seen'), 'hecho' ('done'), 'dicho' ('said').
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All past participles in Spanish end in -ado (-ar verbs) or -ido (-er/-ir verbs).

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the present and perfect tenses to talk about small changes that have a big impact on our lives.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Teachers can end this lesson with a gratitude and micro-habit reflection exercise using sentence stems that clearly distinguish the tenses, e.g. 'Hoy estoy agradecido/a por/porque' and 'Cada día' + verb in the present tense.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The subjunctive indicates uncertainty, wishing or possibility, or refers to actions that have not yet happened.
The conjunction 'para que' translates as 'so that' and is followed by a subjunctive verb.
Spanish uses the subjunctive after 'para que' even though English uses the indicative after 'so that'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: We only use 'para que' + subjunctive to express intentions when the subject of the 2nd verb in the sentence is different from the first. Where the subject is the same in the whole sentence, express intentions with 'para' + infinitive.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: We always use 'para que' + subjunctive to express intentions in Spanish.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the subjunctive after 'para que' to express purpose or intention.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Teachers can increase the level of challenge for Task B2 by asking students to translate the sentence without referring to the hints on the slide. Additionally, an extension could involve asking students to write their own sentence(s) with 'para' and/or 'para que'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Translating word-for-word is an effective strategy when tackling translation tasks.

'Tan ... como' means 'as ... as' in comparisons.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: I can translate 'the best thing was' word-for-word in Spanish.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Many of the most commonly-used Spanish verbs are irregular, e.g. 'ser', 'estar', 'tener', 'hacer', 'venir', 'dar', 'ir'.
The verb 'dar' can be used to describe how something makes people feel. English uses 'to be' + adjective for this.
Indirect object pronouns ('me', 'te', 'le') are used with 'dar' + noun to say how something makes you and others feel.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The verb 'dar' means 'to give, giving' but can also translate as 'to be + adjective' when describing how something makes people feel.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The verb 'dar' always translates as 'to give, giving'.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Frida Kahlo was a Mexican painter known for her vivid self-portraits inspired by pain, identity, and Mexican culture.
Indirect object pronouns replace the person or thing that the action is done to when it is to me, for you, to them, etc.
Indirect object pronouns in Spanish are ‘me’, ‘te’, ‘le’ and ‘le', 'nos', 'os' and 'les'.
Indirect object pronouns can go before the conjugated verb or attach to the infinitive in two-verb constructions.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Spanish word order is different from English. Indirect object pronouns come before the conjugated verb. With 2-verb structures, they can go before the first verb or after the infinitive, attached to it.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Spanish word order is identical to English so I can translate sentences with indirect object pronouns literally from one language to another.

lessons.lessonTitle: Planes de viaje: subjunctive after verbs of emotion

lessonKeywords.description: verb form that indicates actions which are uncertain, wished for, or that have not yet happened; its forms are different from the indicative

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: In Spanish, to express a feeling, emotional reaction or opinion, you often use verbs of emotion.
Verbs of emotion ('gustar', 'encantar', 'dar', 'molestar', etc.) are followed by an infinitive or the subjunctive.
When verbs of emotion are followed by the conjunction 'que', use the subjunctive.
Use a verb of emotion + 'que' + subjunctive for reacting to someone else's action or situation.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Use a verb of emotion + infinitive to react to your own actions. Use a verb of emotion + 'que' + subjunctive to react to someone else’s. Both forms often talk about emotions, but the change of subject triggers the use of subjunctive.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Verbs of emotion like 'gustar', 'encantar', 'dar', 'molestar', etc. are always followed by the infinitive.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the subjunctive after verbs of emotion to talk about travel plans.

teacherTips.teacherTip: After students write about their ideal trip, extend the activity by asking them to react emotionally to someone else’s travel plan using verbs of emotion + 'que' + subjunctive. This puts the grammar in a realistic, communicative context.

verb of necessity or possibility used with a second verb in the infinitive e.g. must, can, want

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: To use comparatives in Spanish, use 'más' or 'menos' + adjective + que'.
To say something is better or worse than something else, use 'mejor que' or 'peor que'.
Modal verbs express necessity or possibility, and can be used to communicate future hopes and desires.
To say what you would like to do, use a modal verb like 'me gustaría' followed by an infinitve.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The stress in 'me gustaría' falls on the 'í'. We can tell this because it has an accent.

lessons.unitTitle: Media and technology: Repaso - la vida diaria y en línea

lessonKeywords.description: tense used to express completed events in the past
tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: To conjugate regular -are verbs in the preterite tense, use the endings -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis, -aron.
To conjugate regular -er/-ir verbs in the preterite tense, use the endings -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis, -ieron.
To conjugate regular -ar verbs in the imperfect tense, use the endings -aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -ábais, -aban.
To conjugate regular -er/-ir verbs in the imperfect tense, use the endings -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían.
The only irregular verbs in the imperfect tense are 'ir' ('iba'), 'ser' ('era') and 'ver' ('veía').

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In Spanish, 'visité' means 'I visited' for a single, completed action in the past. You could also, however, use 'visitaba' to mean 'I visited' for an action that happened repeatedly over a period of time.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The only translation of 'I visited' in Spanish is 'visité'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Conversation answers should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.

lessonKeywords.description: verb tense used to talk about something that used to happen repeatedly and to set the scene in past-tense accounts
verb tense used to talk about what was happening and to set the scene in past-tense accounts
verb tense used to talk about something completed in the past and to drive the narrative forward in past-tense accounts

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The imperfect tense is used for what used to happen repeatedly and to set the scene in past-tense accounts.
The past continuous tense is used for what was happening and to set the scene in past-tense accounts.
The preterite tense is used for something completed in the past and to drive the narrative in past-tense accounts.
It is important to make a plan before producing an extended piece of writing.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The imperfect is used to talk about something that used to happen repeatedly, but it has other uses in different contexts. For example, it can be used to set the scene in a narrative account or story, and to describe general situations in the past.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The imperfect tense is only used to talk about something that used to happen repeatedly.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The 1st, 2nd and 3rd person plural imperfect endings of regular -er and -ir verbs are -íamos, -íais and -ían.
The 1st, 2nd and 3rd person plural imperfect forms of ‘ver’ are ‘veíamos’, ‘veíais’ and ‘veían’.
The 1st, 2nd and 3rd person singular imperfect endings of regular -ar verbs are -aba, -abas and -aba.
The 1st, 2nd and 3rd person singular imperfect endings of regular -er and -ir verbs are -ía, -ías, and -ía.
Regular preterite tense endings are: -é, -aste, -ó for -ar verbs; and -í, -iste, -ió for -er and -ir verbs.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: You should make sure that your answers to reading comprehension questions are specific by locating relevant vocabulary in the text before responding.

lessonKeywords.description: verb tense used to talk about something that used to happen repeatedly
verb tense used to talk about something completed in the past
verb tense used to talk about what was happening
word used to introduce relative clauses, meaning 'when'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: 'iba', 'ibas' and 'iba' are the 1st, 2nd and 3rd person singular imperfect forms of 'ir'. These are irregular.
The preterite tense is used to talk about something completed in the past.
The imperfect tense is used to talk about something that used to happen repeatedly in the past.
The past continuous is created by combining imperfect forms of 'estar' with the present participle.
When 'cuando' indicates an interruption to a past continuous action, the preterite tense is generally used afterwards.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: 'iba' can means 'I used to go' or 'she, he, it used to go'. As 'iba' has several meanings, it’s important to consider to context of the sentence to work out who it refers to.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The only translation of 'iba' is 'I used to go'.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Like ‘ir’, ‘ver’ is irregular in the imperfect tense.
‘veía’, ‘veías’ and ‘veía’ are the 1st, 2nd and 3rd person singular forms of ‘ver’ in the imperfect tense.
The imperfect tense is used to talk about something that used to happen repeatedly in the past.
The imperfect endings of regular -er and -ir verbs are -ía, -ías, -íamos, -íais and -ían.
The preterite tense is used to talk about something completed in the past.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The correct translation of 'I am hungry' is 'tengo hambre'. Sometimes Spanish uses ‘tengo’ + noun where the English would be ‘I am’ + adjective. Other examples of this structure are ‘tengo frío’ (I am cold) and ‘tengo miedo’ (I am scared).
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The correct Spanish translation of 'I am hungry' is 'estoy hambre'.

lessons.lessonTitle: Acciones para un mundo mejor: 'ir' imperfect plural persons
lessons.unitTitle: My neighbourhood: acciones para un mundo mejor

lessonKeywords.description: verb tense used to talk about something that used to happen repeatedly
word used to describe adjectives and verbs
suffix commonly used in Spanish adverbs, meaning -ly

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: ábamos, -abais and -aban are the 1st, 2nd and 3rd person plural endings of -ar verbs in the imperfect tense.
‘ir’ is an irregular verb in the imperfect tense.
-íbamos, -ibais and -iban are the 1st, 2nd and 3rd person plural forms of ‘ir’ in the imperfect tense.
Spanish adverbs ending in -mente (e.g. rápidamente) correspond to English adverbs ending in -ly (e.g. 'quickly').
To form adverbs ending in -mente, add this ending to the feminine form of the adjective (e.g. 'rápida' - 'rápidamente').

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Accents are only present in the 1st person singular (we) form of 'ir' ('íbamos') and -ar verbs (-ábamos) in the imperfect tense.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Accents are present in several forms of 'ir' and -ar verbs in the imperfect tense.

acronym for photo description (people and objects, action, location, mood)

The PALM acronym is a useful prompt to include a range of information when describing photos.

lessons.lessonTitle: Relationships and routines: reflexive 'te'
lessons.unitTitle: Relationships and daily life: personal 'a', pronouns

lessonKeywords.description: sound-symbol correspondence pronounced as in 'gente', meaning 'people'
sound-symbol correspondence pronounced as in 'imaginar', meaning 'to imagine, imagining'
pronoun used to indicate doing something to or for yourself, words like 'myself' and 'yourself'
'myself' in Spanish
'yourself' in Spanish

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The SSC [ge] is pronounced as in ‘gente’ and [gi] as in ‘imaginar’.
When the subject and object of a verb are the same, in Spanish we use reflexive pronouns before the verb e.g. 'Me lavo.'
To say you do something to or for yourself, we use 'te' before the verb in Spanish e.g. 'Te pones un vestido.'
In English we sometimes leave out reflexive pronouns, but we never do in Spanish.
'Me' and 'te' look and sound similar to the possessive adjectives 'mi' and 'tu', but their meanings are different.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: 'Me' and 'te' are reflexive pronouns in Spanish and mean 'myself' and 'yourself' respectively. 'Mi' and 'tu' are the possessive adjectives 'my' and 'your' in Spanish.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: 'Me' and 'te' mean 'my' and 'your' in Spanish.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use verbs with reflexive pronouns 'me' and 'te' to describe my daily routine and ask questions about yours.

teacherTips.teacherTip: When using reflexive pronouns in Spanish, students can sometimes forget that the verb ending still has to change according to the subject of the verb. The dialogue practise in this lesson is useful for emphasising this point.

lessons.lessonTitle: Routines: personal 'a' and contraction 'al'
lessons.unitTitle: Relationships and daily life: personal 'a', pronouns

lessonKeywords.description: preposition placed before a direct object when that object is a specific person or pet
contraction of the preposition 'a' with the article 'el'
adjective that goes before the noun

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: In Spanish we use a personal 'a' between the verb and the direct object if the object is a specific person or pet.
The article 'el' ('the') refers to a singular masculine noun. If personal 'a' is followed by 'el', it becomes 'al'.
Some adjectives come before the noun in Spanish, these are called prenominal adjectives, e.g. 'mismo', 'propio'.
Certain prenominal adjectives, 'bueno', 'primero', 'tercero' and 'malo', lose their -o ending before a masculine noun.
These adjectives may appear in sentences with personal 'a' or 'al', e.g. 'conoces a un buen doctor'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Not all prenominal adjectives ending in -o drop it before a masculine noun, although there are many common ones that do like 'bueno' and 'malo'. However 'segundo' and 'último' do not, and there are others that hold on to their -o too.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All prenominal adjectives ending in -o drop the -o before masculine nouns.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I know how to use personal 'a' with the contraction 'al' and a range of adjectives, to understand and describe routine activities.

teacherTips.teacherTip: For some learners 'human sentences' may help to illustrate grammar. You assign keywords to different pupils who come to the front of the class to translate simple sentences. With the 'a' + 'el' = 'al' rule, 'a' and 'el' will have to sit down to be replaced by 'al' for certain sentences.

lessons.lessonTitle: Routines: personal 'a'
lessons.unitTitle: Relationships and daily life: personal 'a', pronouns

lessonKeywords.description: sound-symbol correspondence pronounced as in ‘ganar’ ('to win')
sound-symbol correspondence pronounced as in ‘domingo’ ('Sunday')
sound-symbol correspondence pronounced as in 'preguntar' ('to question')
person, animal or thing that receives the action of the verb
preposition placed before a direct object when that object is a specific person or pet

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The SSC [ga] is pronounced as in 'ganar', [go] is pronounced as in 'domingo' and [gu] is pronounced as in 'preguntar'.
A direct object is the person, animal or thing that receives the action of the verb.
When a direct object is a person or pet, Spanish uses the personal 'a' after the verb, e.g. 'cuido a mi gato'.
For other direct objects it is not necessary, e.g 'cuido mi casa'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In Spanish you use the personal 'a' after the verb when the following direct object is a specific person or an animal we have a name for (a pet).
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: In Spanish the personal 'a' is required between verbs and all direct objects.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the personal 'a' between verbs and people or pets as direct objects, to describe routine activities.

teacherTips.teacherTip: In this lesson the Spanish personal 'a' is introduced. As part of a plenary you could consider a fun 'call and response' activity where you say a noun and if it needs a personal 'a' the pupils hold up their arms in an A shape. If it doesn't, pupils should stay completely still.

lessons.lessonTitle: Relationships and routines: reflexive 'me'
lessons.unitTitle: Relationships and daily life: personal 'a', pronouns

lessonKeywords.description: pronoun used to indicate doing something to or for yourself, words like 'myself' and 'yourself'
'myself' in Spanish
verb used with a reflexive pronoun when the subject and object of the action are the same

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Spanish verbs like ‘despertar’ have a stem change in some of their forms, e.g. ‘despierto’ is the 1st person singular.
The word ‘demasiado’ can be both adjective and adverb. As an adverb it needs no agreement but as an adjective it does.
When a direct object is a specific person or pet, in Spanish the personal ‘a’ goes after the verb, e.g. ‘veo a la niña'.
Sometimes the subject and object of a verb are the same. Use a reflexive pronoun before the verb, e.g. 'me lavo'.
When subject and object of verbs are the same, Spanish always uses a reflexive pronoun. English does not always do this.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: When the action of a verb is directed towards the self, Spanish always uses a reflexive pronoun. English does not always do this; for example, 'me levanto a las siete' - 'I get up at seven'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: If you use 'me' in Spanish you need 'myself' in English.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use verbs with the reflexive pronoun ‘me’ for routine activities that I do for myself, and verbs with the personal 'a' for actions I do to and for others.

teacherTips.teacherTip: It's helpful to contrast reflexive and non-reflexive verb use so pupils understand that most verbs can have reflexive and non-reflexive meanings, e.g. knowing that 'llamo a Lucía' means 'I call Lucía' whilst 'me llamo Lucía' is 'I'm called Lucía (I call myself Lucía)' avoids misunderstanding.

lessons.lessonTitle: What I have to do: singular modal verbs
lessons.unitTitle: What we can and must do: -AR verbs 1st person plural, modals 'poder' 'deber'

lessonKeywords.description: verbs of necessity and possibility used with a 2nd verb in the infinitive, e.g. must, can, want
modal verb that means to have to, must with singular forms ‘debo’ - I must, ‘debes’ - you must, ‘debe’ - she, he, it must.
modal verb that means to be able to, can, with singular forms ‘puedo’ - I can, ‘puedes’ - you can, ‘puede’ - she, he, it can
modal verb that means to want, wanting with singular forms ‘quiero’ - I want, ‘quieres’ - you want, ‘quiere’ - she, he, it wants.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The SSC [ca] is pronounced as in 'casa', [co] as in ‘comer’ and [cu] as in ‘cuerpo.
The modal verb ‘deber’ means ‘must’ and we use it to talk about obligations.
The modal verb ‘poder’ means ‘can/be able to’ and we use it to talk about possibility.
The modal verb ‘querer’ means ‘to want, wanting’ and we use it to talk about what we want to do.
All modal verbs are followed by an infinitive.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In Spanish there is a difference between them: 'sí' with an accent means 'yes', and 'si' without an accent means 'if'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The word 'si' means both 'yes' and 'if'.

lessonKeywords.description: pronounced as in 'pero'
pronounced as in 'perro'
pronoun referring to the person or thing that is indirectly affected by the verb; in English, this includes '(to, for) me'
type of verb that appears after an indirect object pronoun

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: In Spanish, r is pronounced differently depending on its position in the word and whether it is single or double.
Word-initial 'r' is rolled and pronounced as in 'rojo'. It sounds identical to the 'rr' in 'perro'.
'Gustar'-type verbs commonly appear after the indirect object pronoun 'me'.
'Gustar'-type verbs agree with the subject in number: -a for a singular noun and -an for a plural noun.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: 'Me gusta' is 'I like' for a singular or uncountable noun, but plural nouns require 'me gustan'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: 'Me gusta' is always the correct way to say 'I like'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use 'gustar'-type verbs to give my opinion about sport.

teacherTips.teacherTip: When introducing 'gustar'-type verbs, it can be useful to draw pupils' attention to the literal translation of a phrase and to the more natural English equivalent.

lessonKeywords.description: replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to; in English, this includes '(to/for) me'
type of verb that appears after an indirect object pronoun
preposition placed before a direct object when that object is a specific person or animal we have a name for

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Word-initial 'r' is rolled and pronounced as in 'rojo'. It sounds identical to the 'rr' in 'perro'.
Gustar-type verbs commonly appear after an indirect object pronoun like 'me' or 'le'.
We use the personal 'a' before the object if it's a person or animal.
There are two frequently used word orders in Spanish: subject + verb + object and object + verb + subject.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In Spanish, unlike in English, the object can go before or after the verb.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: In Spanish, like in English, the object always goes after the verb.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use gustar-type verbs and the personal 'a' in the context of pets and animals.

lessonKeywords.description: informal way to address 'you'
formal way to address 'you'
formal way to address 'you all'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: We can boost our word knowledge by making connections between words such as word families, synonyms, opposites, etc.
To mean 'you' in an informal context, use 'tú'. In a formal context, use 'usted'.

'Usted' and 'ustedes' respectively take the 3rd person singular and plural forms of the verb.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: There are two ways to mean 'you (singular)' in Spanish. Use 'tú' to mean 'you' in an informal context, and 'usted' to mean 'you' in a formal context.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: In Spanish there are two verbs for 'to be'. Use 'estar' for location, state or mood and 'ser' for permanent traits.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: 'Desde hace' means 'for' and it appears together with the present tense to say how long we've been doing something.
'Hace' means 'ago' and we use it with the past.

The BORDER acronym is a useful tool to respond fully and accurately to bullet point writing prompts.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: BORDER is also a very useful strategy for extended pieces of writing. Simply apply it to each paragraph separately. This will help you respond clearly and completely to each bullet point.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Using a checklist before a read-aloud task is a powerful and effective strategy.
In a read-aloud task, think carefully about how to correctly pronounce the letters in each word and spot tricky sounds.
Considering cognates and mentally rehearsing the text are key steps in preparation for a read-aloud task.
We can avoid distractors by not rushing to select an answer.
Distractors can appear anywhere - in the question, the answer options or the text itself.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Simply re-reading without purpose doesn’t necessarily lead to better comprehension. Strategies such as reading through the text and questions, using each question to find the relevant part of the text, avoiding distractors, etc., are more effective.

lessons.lessonTitle: Visita de un instituo español: irregular superlatives 'el mejor', 'el peor'
lessons.unitTitle: Studying and my future: en el instituto

lessonKeywords.description: pronounced as in 'gente'
pronounced as in 'imaginar'
pronounced as in 'ojo'
specifies a particular noun, indicating 'this', 'that', 'these' or 'those'
form of an adjective or adverb used to express the highest or lowest degree of a quality, e.g. 'the tallest', 'the least interesting'

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: [ge] is pronounced as in 'gente', [gi] is pronounced as in 'imaginar' and [j] is pronounced as in 'ojo'.
Demonstrative adjectives indicate a particular noun and they must agree with this noun in gender and number.
Adjectives ending in -z, -e, and -ista have have the plural endings -ces, -es and -istas.
'el mejor', 'el peor', 'el mayor' and 'el menor' are common irregular superlatives.
Superlatives must agree with the nouns they describe in gender and number.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The superlative 'el mejor' must agree with the noun it describes in number and gender. Its other forms are 'la mejor', 'los mejores' and 'las mejores'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The only translation of 'the best' in Spanish is 'el mejor'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use common superlatives in the context of life at school.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Exit Quiz Qs 5-6 and Learning Cycle 3 contain Higher Tier grammar and vocabulary. You could consider using mini whiteboards for Task B2 to assess for whole-class understanding and improvise additional sentences if necessary.

lessons.lessonTitle: Visita de un instituo español: possessive adjectives and pronouns
lessons.unitTitle: Studying and my future: en el instituto

lessonKeywords.description: adjective that identifies ownership of a noun
word that replaces a noun and identifies its ownership

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Possessive adjectives identify ownership of a noun, e.g. 'my', 'mine'.
Possessive adjectives must agree with the nouns they describe in gender and number.
The possessive adjectives 'mi', 'tu' and 'su' come before nouns. 'mío', 'tuyo' and 'suyo' come after nouns for emphasis.
Possessive pronouns replace nouns and identify ownership e.g. mine, yours.
The possessive pronouns 'el mío', 'el tuyo' and 'el suyo' have masculine, feminine, singular and plural forms.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: When referring to body parts, Spanish speakers replace possessive adjectives with definite articles, e.g. 'me he roto el brazo'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The Spanish translation of 'I've broken my arm' is 'me he roto mi brazo'. You use the possessive adjective for body parts.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use possessive adjectives and possessive pronouns in the context of life at school.

lessons.lessonTitle: Local and international events: present continuous
lessons.unitTitle: Important events: present and imperfect continuous

lessonKeywords.description: describes events happening right now: 'I am doing'
specifies a particular noun, indicating 'this', 'that', 'these' or 'those'
pronoun, e.g. 'que' that introduces a relative clause

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: In Spanish, the sounds [b] and [v] are the same, as in 'abuela' and 'verde', so we need to learn spellings by heart.
To say what is happening now, we use the verb 'estar' with a present participle; this is called the present continuous.
The present participle is formed by removing the infinitive ending and adding -ando for -ar verbs and -iendo for others.
To say 'these' for masculine nouns we use 'estos' and for feminine nouns 'estas'; these are demonstrative adjectives.
Relative pronoun 'que' means 'who' or 'that'. 'Donde' means 'where'; there is no accent when it's a relative pronoun.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Accents are really important in Spanish. The 'tú' form of 'estar' has an accent on the á: 'estás' (you are) whereas the demonstrative adjective for plural feminine nouns, 'estas' does not: 'estas flores' (these flowers).
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The feminine plural demonstrative adjective for 'these' is the same as the 'tú' form of the verb 'estar'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe what I and others are doing at events now using the present continuous.

teacherTips.teacherTip: To adapt the final speaking activity C4 for pupils who need more support, teachers could provide the full Spanish sentences, so that the second pupil completes the table without the first pupil having to translate the sentence from English into Spanish first.

lessons.lessonTitle: News events: -ar verbs preterite tense for interruptions
lessons.unitTitle: Important events: present and imperfect continuous

lessonKeywords.description: preposition meaning 'from' and 'of'
verb tense used to describe events happening right now, e.g. ‘I am doing’
verb tense used to talk about ongoing actions in the past, what was happening
verb tense used for events completed in the past

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The preposition 'de' joins two nouns to describe a type of something, e.g. ‘un billete de avión’ ('a plane ticket').
We use 'estar' in the present tense + present participle to talk about ongoing events; this is the present continuous.
'Estar' in the imperfect + present participle describes what someone was doing; this is the imperfect continuous.
Sometimes an action interrupts what someone was doing. We use 'cuando' followed by the preterite to express this.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Different past tenses describe different elements of a story. The imperfect continuous describes what was happening ('Estaba corriendo ...') then the preterite tense describes an interruption to that activity ('... cuando llegó una vaca'.).
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: When telling a story about a past event, I have to keep the full account in the same past tense.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe past news events using the imperfect continuous with ‘cuando’ ('when') and the preterite tense for interruptions.

teacherTips.teacherTip: To help students express their full imagination for the final written activity (task C2), access to a bilingual dictionary would be useful.

lessons.lessonTitle: News events: present and imperfect continuous
lessons.unitTitle: Important events: present and imperfect continuous

lessonKeywords.description: describes events happening right now, e.g. 'I am doing'
verb tense used to talk about ongoing actions in the past, what was happening
verb meaning 'to be', also the auxiliary verb for the present and imperfect continuous tenses

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The sound-spelling correspondences [n] and [ñ] are pronounced differently: like the [n] in 'poner' and the [ñ] in 'año'.
'Estar' means 'to be' and is used to express a state or location. 'You are' is 'estás' and 'you were' is 'estabas'.
We use 'estar' in the present + present participle to describe ongoing events. This is called the present continuous.
We use 'estar' in the imperfect + present participle to describe past ongoing events; this is the imperfect continuous.
The present participle stays the same: remove the infinitive ending and add -ando for -ar verbs and -iendo for -er/-ir.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The 'I' and 'he, she, it' forms of the imperfect tense of 'estar' are the same: 'estaba'. Therefore you have to use the context to work out who the subject of the verb is when this form is being used.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: In the imperfect continuous I can tell who the subject of the verb is by looking at the form of 'estar' being used.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe ongoing events in the present and the past, using the present and imperfect continuous tenses.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The final C4 speaking task can be adapted by providing person A/B with the full Spanish phrases to read aloud rather than having to translate from English first.

lessons.lessonTitle: Local and international events: imperfect continuous
lessons.unitTitle: Important events: present and imperfect continuous

lessonKeywords.description: verb tense used to talk about ongoing actions in the past, what 'was happening'
I was/he, she, it was
you (singular) were

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: We can create nouns in Spanish by adding -idad to singular adjectives ending in a consonant. E.g. real to realidad.
The singular forms of 'estar' in the imperfect tense are 'estaba' (I was or he, she, was) and 'estabas' (you were).
To talk about ongoing events in the past we use 'estar' in the imperfect tense with a present participle.
The preterite is used for completed actions, remove the -ar verb ending and add -é (I), -aste (you) or -ó (he, she, it).
We can combine these two tenses to describe events in the past: 'Estaba escuchando la radio cuando noté un olor raro.'

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: To form the imperfect continuous, only the form of 'estar' needs to change, into the imperfect tense. The present participle stays the same, it is formed by removing the infinitive ending and adding -ando for -ar verbs and -iendo for all other verbs.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: To form the imperfect continuous instead of the present continuous both the form of 'estar' and the present participle need to change.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe past events using the imperfect continuous combined with the preterite tense.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Teaching the combination of the imperfect continuous and the preterite tense lends itself well to storytelling games in pairs or small groups. You can start off with a set phrase like 'Estaba caminando en el bosque cuando ....' and then the other people in the group add further description.

lessonKeywords.description: verb that doesn’t refer to a particular person or thing
form of verb used to express what would happen
acronym used to respond fully and accurately to bullet point writing prompts

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: 'Hay que', 'se debe', 'se puede' and 'se necesita' are impersonal verbs.
Examples of impersonal uses of verbs are ‘basta (con)’, ‘falta’, ‘hace falta’, ‘parece’ and ‘vale la pena’.
These impersonal verbs are used without a subject and followed by an infinitive.
To conjugate the conditional, add -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -iáis, and -ían to the infinitive.
The BORDER acronym is a useful tool to respond fully and accurately to bullet point writing prompts.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Verbs like 'basta' and 'hace falta' can’t always be translated word-for-word - they don’t work the same way as English verbs. You need to choose the most idiomatic or natural-sounding translation based on the context.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: I can translate verbs like 'basta' and 'hace falta' word-for-word.

lessons.lessonTitle: Consejos de vida: singular affirmative commands, role-play (AQA)

lessonKeywords.description: form of verbs used to give instructions or commands

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Use the affirmative imperative to tell somebody to do something or to give instructions.
For 'tú' commands, use -a for -ar verbs and -e for -er/-ir verbs in the affirmative imperative: habla, come, escribe.
Irregular imperative verbs include: 'sé', 've', 'ten', 'ven', 'haz', 'di', 'pon', 'sal'.
To form the familiar affirmative imperative of reflexive verbs, add the pronoun 'te' along with any necessary accents.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: When talking to somebody familiar to you ('tú') with the affirmative imperative of an -ar verb, use the ending -a, and for an -er or -ir verb, use the ending -e. Irregular imperative verbs include: 'sé', 've', 'ten', 'ven', 'haz', 'di', 'pon', 'sal'.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: To give an order or command to 'tú' (you, informal), you should use the 2nd person singular form of the verb.
